### I was a skilled consultant and business analyst, worked with clients my whole career in IT and business projects, so problem-solving was basically in my DNA. All the UX courses I took were addition to this: how to interview, why to put the user first and how to create prototypes.
**According to my current role, I am an experience designer, which is a fine mixture of the roles of a UX researcher, UX designer, service designer, business analyst and project manager.**

I have always explained my role to those, who are not familiar with the term UX designer, that this is a type of consultancy (as I was a consultant for nearly a decade, this was the thing my family was familiar with 🙂). Finally, a role, where I can utilize all my skills I learned as a consultant. I could say I was lucky, but I honestly think that the generalist state-of-mind like mine is the thing that differentiates us from other agencies.

Most of us, experience designers at [Works.](https://worksdot.hu/) are generalists. There is a skillset which is essential in this role: being able to talk to clients, conduct user interviews, synthesize problems, and come up with possible solutions.
**We help our clients to achieve their business goals with the help of UX, business analyst and project management tools and expertise.**
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_is_the_ux_designer_a_dying_breed_mlfg5_2_b1ae069cfb.jpg

1. **UX:**it is a must to be familiar with the typical user behavior, the UX principles, design processes and building up simple to more complex low-fidelity prototypes. The skills mentioned above could be easily linked: UX research and design go hand in hand to create products that users love and use. Also, it is essential to present these ideas on a client workshop to stakeholders, to articulate our findings and solutions.
2. On the other hand, the role of a business analyst or project manager might be odd in an experience designer’s guidebook.**A business analyst makes sure that the design meets the client’s expectations**, and the requirements are aligned with the design. We map processes, create [state diagrams](https://medium.com/works/how-state-diagram-can-help-designers-fa13a7f8207f) and all the documentation necessary to comprehend the design, so that the clients can understand, and the developers can create the product.
3. **As for project management:** well, this is the thing everybody hates from the bottom of their heart (mine included). For me, project management consists of communication, managing tasks, problem-solving and project documentation (such as meeting minutes, retrospectives etc.). None can simply imagine working on a design project without the above, to be able to deliver the project on time.

But this does not mean that all of us are equally skilled in writing lengthy business specifications, building a prototypes or analyzing data from quantitative research. And that is all fine, because we are a team of people with different knowledge and interests.

***Nonetheless as an agency, we strive to build-up the most basic skillset of our junior experience designers from the ground up: research, managing their own time and tasks and then widen it afterwards.****Research is the foundation that every UX designer can rely on getting in touch with the users, empathizing with their needs and problems are the key to good UX design.*

The role of the business analyst is often referred to bridge between business and IT. As an experience designer I believe I am bridging the gap between the users, clients, keeping in mind that the design, always should be feasible for development.

**Therefore, the experience designer is more, than a business analyst and more, than a UX designer in one person.** *Of course, all this does not mean that a design project is a one-man-show as all of us needs to get feedback and ideate from time to time within the team.*

Therefore, we ensure that always at least two experience designers work on a project, so they can learn from each other and strengthen each other’s skillsets. One thing is for sure: every one of us in the design team needs to have the basic knowledge of our users, the business and design process and methods while managing their own projects.

What about UI design? In the agency model, where we parallelly work on different project for our clients, it is hard to be a UX and a UI designer at the same time. UI design requires the creative work (suc as mockups, moodboards) and the creation of many screens and design systems, whilst a UX designer must focus on the big picture: the concept, the information architecture, the journeys and so on.

**Because of the different approaches and not the required skillset, it is inadmissible, even impossible to do the UX and UI work at the same time.** *If you are lucky enough to do one after the other, that’s fine, but agencies typically don’t work that way.*

Someone who only does UX might be a dying breed, as more and more skills are needed to become successful in the field. In the coming years, these roles might disappear completely as companies begin to realize the benefits of a generalist experience designer. But how can courses and trainings prepare the new entrants for such a challenge? In the next article, we are going to elaborate on this further.

blogPosts.title: How state diagram can help designers?
blogPosts.excerpt: State diagram (or state-transition diagram or state model) sounds like an engineering buzzword from the 80s, however this is a very powerful tool UX/UI designers could use in their projects.
blogPosts.imageAlt: How state diagram can help designers?

content.content:
State diagram (or state-transition diagram or state model) sounds like an engineering buzzword from the 80s, however this is a very powerful tool UX/UI designers could use in their projects. In a UX/UI design project, where UX is focusing on the journey, UI is actually focusing on states and state-transitions. A state diagram is quite flexible, you can make it fit your needs. Bonus: developers can understand it easily. Let’s see what it is and how you can use it.

### What is a state diagram?

A state diagram is a representation tool “used to describe and analyze the different possible states of an entity within a system” (Business analyst body of knowledge, v3, 2015). An entity can be any object within a system, depending on what system you are designing or analyzing. In a design system the entity is already very well defined: it is called a component, e.g. a color, a button, a header, a table, a page.

A state is also a known definition in UI design: e.g., a button can have a pressed state and a default state. Not all components have different states, typically a primary color does not have states, but the components which use this primary color might have. Those entities can have states which “do” something either by themselves or as a result of a user action. The basket in a webshop can be empty or not empty, a field on a form can be active or inactive, etc. More complex components can also have states: a search result list can be empty and in this state it might behave differently compared to the state when there are results in the list.

A component which can have multiple states might go through these states in a predefined sequence, and in most cases going from one state to another state follows some rules. Eg. in a webshop the empty basket cannot have the state “paid”, first it needs to contain something. An inactive button cannot have pressed state, first it needs to be active. So when there are several states of a component, not all transitions (going from one state to another) are valid.

In a state diagram we use boxes to represent states and arrows to represent valid state transitions. State diagrams are kind of complementary methods of the activity diagrams: on activity diagram the boxes represent activities (transitions) and the arrows show the states.

Let’s see an example. We were doing the design in a document management system implementation project for a pharma company. In this system the document could have the following states:

- **Edit**: from the point the user created the document they can edit it. Until the point the owner of the document sends it for approval, we consider it as under editing.
- **Waiting for approval**: In this state the document cannot be edited and it is at the managers who can either approve or reject it. Once it is approved, it moves to approved phase. Once it is rejected, it goes back to editing.
- **Approved, waiting for signature**: When all approvers approved the document, it goes for another managerial level to be signed. Signers can still reject it, then it goes back to editing. Or all signatures are collected, then it moves to signed state.
- **Signed**: All signers gave their signature, the document can be distributed in-house or sent back to the vendor, depending on the nature of the document. It cannot be edited any more, it is a “final” version.
- **Invalid**: It might happen that a new version of the same document gets all the signatures (eg. imagine an internal holiday policy), the previous version of the document will be invalid.

Let’s see how these steps look on a state diagram:
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_state_diagram_can_help_designers_1_35afbf25ed.png
content.caption: A state diagram showing an example from a document management system
content.alt: A state diagram showing an example from a document management system

content.content:
### How can we use a state diagram?

Any representation methods are just recommendations. We can adjust them to our needs. No teacher stands behind you to check how precisely you are using a state diagram. Business analysts love standardizing their tools, but simply because there is a formal spelling book of your language does not mean you cannot say what and how you want. I’ll show what I mean.

The state diagram in the above format might look handy at first, but it is difficult to add other information to it. So first lets make it one-dimensional, lets flatten it. It means that the states will be in one row — it might result in too many arrows around them, but we pay this price.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_state_diagram_can_help_designers_2_850fb8490c.png
content.caption: State diagram with the same content as above, but this version is “flattened”
content.alt: State diagram with the same content as above, but this version is “flattened”

content.content:
Now we can add another dimension to our diagram, so it will become a matrix. I’d recommend adding the components in the other dimension, in this way we can show how each component looks like in each states. You can simply add a description, or you can add the graphical versions to the matrix, it depends what is easier to understand and to create. I’d recommend to put only those components on this matrix, that are changing according to the states, and do not put all the components to the matrix to avoid it to be too big and unusable.

Also we can add functionalities in the other dimensions, and show which user group have rights to access the functionalities in each states.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_state_diagram_can_help_designers_3_4076621144.png
content.caption: State diagram with an additional dimension showing user rigths in each state
content.alt: State diagram with an additional dimension showing user rigths in each state

content.content:
This way we get a user rights matrix, and developers will be extremely happy. Another benefit of this user rights vs. state matrix is that there is no gap, since the matrix contains all functions and all states (and we filled all cells of the matrix), there can be no special case we did not think about.

The good news is that the two previous matrices can also be combined: the states, the main components and the privileges can all be put on one matrix.

### How state diagram helps design?

I believe state diagrams are natural tools of UI design process. In UX we focus on the customer journey, which is an activity-oriented approach. From the point we need to design the final screens, we need to change our mindset to a state-oriented approach, to build up the UI components and to define how each screens need to behave. People are doing processes, screens have states. When we already have the journeys and screen-flows defined, we need to distill the states of these components. In some cases these states are trivial (active vs inactive state of a button), but in case of more complex components or more complex processes, these states are far from being trivial. So you need a good tool to collect, describe and represent these states: this is state diagram.

A state diagram is also a quality control tool: once you identified all possible states of the main components, you will see if you have thought of all states of the smaller components. A state diagram in this approach is a double-check tool, a frame which need to be filled out.

State diagram also helps in the communication with the developers, as they tend to try to find the gaps in your process-oriented design. Once you have defined all the states and all components are defined in each state: there is no gap, and the developer is happy, which is half the success.

services.subtitle: MINDEN JÓ DÖNTÉS A MEGÉRTÉSSEL KEZDŐDIK
services.heroDescription: Valós felhasználói insightokra építjük a digitális döntéseket, hogy a fejlesztések ne feltételezésekre, hanem bizonyítékokra épüljenek.

definitionSection.heading: Mi az a UX kutatás?
definitionSection.description: A UX kutatás (felhasználói élmény kutatás) egy módszertan, amellyel feltárjuk, hogyan gondolkodnak, éreznek és viselkednek a felhasználók egy digitális termék használata közben. Interjúk, tesztek és adatelemzés segítségével valós bizonyítékokat gyűjtünk, hogy a termékfejlesztési döntések ne megérzéseken, hanem tényeken alapuljanak. Az eredmény: kevesebb felesleges fejlesztés, jobb felhasználói élmény és mérhető üzleti eredmények.

intro.heading: Milyen kérdésekre segítünk választ találni?

projectExamplesIntro.heading: Kiemelt projektek
projectExamplesIntro.description: Néhány projekt, ahol a kutatás kézzelfogható üzleti eredményt hozott.

intro.heading: Amit érdemes tisztázni a kutatás előtt
intro.description: A UX kutatás mindig egy konkrét döntési helyzetből indul ki. A projekt célja, a rendelkezésre álló idő és a megválaszolandó kérdések határozzák meg, milyen kutatási megközelítés ad valóban használható eredményt. Ezek a leggyakoribb kérdések, amelyek a közös munka előtt gyakran felmerülnek.

items.question: Mikor érdemes UX kutatást végezni?
items.answer: Akkor, amikor egy digitális döntésnek tétje van, de még nincs elég bizonyíték a jó irányhoz. Például új termék vagy funkció előtt, redesign előtt, konverziós problémák esetén, vagy amikor a csapatban sok a vélemény, de kevés a felhasználói visszajelzés. Egy jól időzített kutatás segít elkerülni, hogy időt és pénzt fordítsatok egy rossz irányba induló fejlesztésre.

items.question: Kell már kész termék vagy prototípus a kutatáshoz?
items.answer: Nem feltétlenül. UX kutatást lehet végezni kész terméken, kattintható prototípuson, korai koncepción, szolgáltatási folyamaton vagy akár még fejlesztés előtti ötleteken is. Más módszert választunk akkor, ha egy meglévő felület problémáit keressük, és mást akkor, ha egy új ötlet életképességét szeretnénk validálni.

items.question: Hány felhasználóra van szükség?
items.answer: Ez a kutatási kérdéstől függ. Kvalitatív kutatásnál gyakran már kisebb mintával is kirajzolódnak a legfontosabb mintázatok. Ha több célcsoportot, eltérő használati helyzeteket vagy számszerűsíthető eredményeket kell vizsgálni, nagyobb mintára lehet szükség.

items.question: Mennyi ideig tart egy UX kutatási projekt?
items.answer: Egy fókuszált kutatás akár néhány hét alatt is lefuthat, egy összetettebb discovery vagy ügyfélélmény-kutatás viszont hosszabb időt igényelhet. Az időtartamot főleg a kutatási cél, a célcsoport elérhetősége, a módszertan és az elemzés mélysége határozza meg.

items.question: Online is működik a kutatás?
items.answer: Igen, sok kutatási helyzetben kifejezetten jól működik az online kutatás. Interjúk, használhatósági tesztek, koncepcióvalidációk és workshopok is végezhetők távolról. Vannak helyzetek, amikor a személyes jelenlét többet ad, például fizikai környezethez vagy ügyféltéri élményhez kapcsolódó kutatásoknál.

items.question: Hogyan választotok kutatási módszert?
items.answer: Nem módszerből indulunk ki, hanem a döntési kérdésből. Először tisztázzuk, mire kell választ kapni: új igényeket szeretnénk feltárni, meglévő problémát megérteni, koncepciót validálni vagy használhatósági hibákat azonosítani. Ehhez választjuk ki a megfelelő kutatási megközelítést.

definitionSection.heading: Mi az a UX/UI design?
definitionSection.description: A UX/UI design a digitális termékek működésének és megjelenésének tervezése. A UX, vagyis a felhasználói élmény azt tervezi meg, hogyan használják a terméket: milyen a felhasználó útja, a folyamatok és a struktúra. A UI, vagyis a felhasználói felület azt, hogyan néz ki: a vizuális megjelenés, a komponensek, a részletek. A kettő együtt adja, hogy a termék egyszerre legyen könnyen használható és igényes, a felhasználónak és az üzletnek is.

intro.description: Ha ezek a kérdések nálatok is felmerültek, a tervezés a következő logikus lépés.

cards.title: „Hogyan lehet egyszerűbb egy bonyolult folyamat?”
cards.description: Segítünk újragondolni a felhasználói utakat, hogy kevesebb bizonytalansággal és kevesebb lépésben érjék el a céljukat ügyfeleid.

cards.title: „Hogyan fejlődjön a termék anélkül, hogy egyre bonyolultabbá válna?”
cards.description: Úgy tervezzük tovább a terméked, hogy az új funkciók ne növeljék a komplexitást, hanem természetesen illeszkedjenek a meglévő élménybe.

cards.title: „Hogyan tervezzünk egységes, konzisztens élményt több felületen?”
cards.description: Összehangoljuk a működési logikát és a vizuális megjelenést, hogy a felhasználók minden felületen ugyanarra az élményre számíthassanak.

cards.title: „Hogyan csökkenthetjük a felhasználói hibákat és a lemorzsolódást?”
cards.description: A felületeket úgy tervezzük meg, hogy azok természetesen vezessék végig a felhasználót a végrehajtás lépésein.

cards.title: Egyszerűsítjük a felhasználói folyamatokat

items.answer: Akkor, amikor egy digitális terméket vagy folyamatot használhatóbbá, egyértelműbbé és következetesebbé szeretnétek tenni — új fejlesztés, redesign, vagy egy összetetté vált felület esetén.

items.question: Milyen részletességű terveket készítetek?

items.question: Fejlesztés előtt vagy közben is érdemes UX/UI tervezőt bevonni?

Ugyanakkor már futó vagy fejlesztés alatt álló projektekbe is be tudunk kapcsolódni, és úgy fejlesztjük tovább a meglévő megoldást, hogy az jobban szolgálja a felhasználókat és az üzleti célokat.

items.question: Részt vesztek a fejlesztési folyamatban is?

items.question: Mikor van szükség Service Design projektre?
items.answer: Akkor, amikor a problémát nem lehet egyetlen digitális felület áttervezésével megoldani. Ha az ügyfélélményt több csapat, folyamat vagy csatorna együtt alakítja, a fejlesztéshez a teljes szolgáltatást érdemes újragondolni.

items.question: Miben más ez, mint egy UX projekt?
items.answer: A UX kutatás segít megérteni a felhasználókat. A UX/UI design megtervezi a digitális felületet. A Service Design ezekre építve a teljes szolgáltatás működését vizsgálja: hogyan kapcsolódnak össze a folyamatok, a csapatok és az érintkezési pontok egy egységes ügyfélélménnyé.

items.question: Kiket érdemes bevonni?
items.answer: A Service Design akkor működik igazán jól, ha nemcsak a digitális csapat vesz részt benne. Jellemzően üzleti területek, ügyfélszolgálat, operáció, marketing és más érintett szervezeti egységek is bekapcsolódnak a közös tervezésbe.

items.question: Mennyi ideig tart egy projekt?
items.answer: Ez a szolgáltatás összetettségétől és a projekt céljától függ. Egy fókuszált fejlesztési projekt néhány hét alatt is lezárható, míg egy komplex szolgáltatás vagy működési modell újratervezése több hónapot is igényelhet.

items.question: Mi történik a workshopok után?
items.answer: A workshopok nem a projekt végét jelentik, hanem a közös tervezés alapját. Az ott születő felismeréseket rendszerezzük, kidolgozzuk a jövőbeni működést, és konkrét fejlesztési roadmapet készítünk a megvalósításhoz.

items.question: Hogyan kapcsolódik a digitális fejlesztésekhez?
items.answer: A digitális felület a szolgáltatás egyik fontos része, de ritkán az egyetlen. A Service Design segít meghatározni, hogy a digitális fejlesztések hogyan illeszkedjenek a teljes működésbe, így a felhasználói élmény és a háttérfolyamatok együtt fejlődnek.

definitionSection.heading: Mi az az AI-alapú digitális termékfejlesztés?
definitionSection.description: Az AI-alapú digitális termékfejlesztés azt jelenti, hogy a mesterséges intelligenciát eszközként használjuk egy üzleti probléma megoldására, nem célként. Megkeressük, hol tud az AI valódi értéket teremteni: hol takarít meg időt, költséget vagy emberi munkát. items.question: Mikor érdemes AI-alapú digitális termékfejlesztésben gondolkodni?
items.answer: Akkor, amikor van egy konkrét üzleti problémád vagy ötleted, amelyre működő digitális megoldást keresel — és gyorsan szeretnél eljutni a kézzelfogható eredményig. Az AI itt eszköz: a fejlesztést gyorsítja és a kockázatot csökkenti, de a fókusz mindig a megoldandó problémán van.

items.question: Kell már kész specifikációval rendelkeznünk?
items.answer: Nem. Elég, ha az üzleti probléma vagy a cél megvan — a megoldás formáját közösen alakítjuk ki. Sokszor épp az a projekt első értéke, hogy tisztázzuk, valójában mit érdemes megépíteni.

items.question: Milyen digitális termékeket készítetek?
items.answer: Belső eszközöket, prototípusokat, automatizált folyamatokat, adat- és ügyfélélmény-alapú alkalmazásokat — mindig az adott üzleti problémához igazítva. Nem egy technológiát erőltetünk rá, hanem a megfelelő megoldást választjuk.

items.question: Mikor érdemes AI-ban gondolkodni és mikor nem?
items.answer: Nem minden üzleti problémára az AI a legjobb megoldás. Először mindig a problémát, a folyamatot és az üzleti célt értjük meg — és ha az AI valódi előnyt jelent, segítünk megtalálni a megfelelő megoldást. Ha viszont egy egyszerűbb vagy hagyományos digitális megoldás vezet gyorsabban eredményre, azt fogjuk javasolni. Technológiafüggetlen partnerként mindig a problémából indulunk ki, nem a technológiából.

items.question: Tudtok együtt dolgozni a meglévő fejlesztőcsapatunkkal?
items.answer: Igen. Sok esetben épp ez a cél: mi felgyorsítjuk a korai, bizonytalan szakaszt egy validált, működő verzióval, amit a saját csapatod tud továbbfejleszteni és üzemeltetni. A megoldást átadható formában készítjük.

items.question: Mi történik a prototípus elkészülte után?
items.answer: A működő első verziót közösen értékeljük: mit tanultunk, mi vált be, mi az irány. Innen dönthettek a továbbfejlesztésről, az éles bevezetésről vagy az átadásról. A prototípus nem a végállomás, hanem egy megalapozott döntési pont.

definitionSection.heading: Mi az a digitális akadálymentesítés?
definitionSection.description: A digitális akadálymentesítés azt jelenti, hogy egy weboldal vagy alkalmazás mindenki számára használható: a látás-, hallás- vagy mozgássérült felhasználóknak, az idősebb korosztálynak és az átmeneti korlátozottsággal élőknek is. A nemzetközi WCAG szabvány alapján auditáljuk és javítjuk a felületeket, így a termék nemcsak a jogszabályi elvárásoknak felel meg, hanem szélesebb közönséget is elér.

intro.heading: Amit érdemes tisztázni az audit előtt
intro.description: Nincs két egyforma digitális szolgáltatás. A termék, a célok és a jelenlegi működés határozza meg, hogyan dolgozunk együtt. Ezek a leggyakoribb kérdések, amelyek a közös munka előtt felmerülnek.

items.question: Mikor érdemes akadálymentesítéssel foglalkozni?
items.answer: A legjobb, ha már a tervezés és fejlesztés elején, mert így elkerülhető a későbbi, költséges áttervezés. De egy meglévő szolgáltatásnál sem késő: auditból indulva, priorizált lépésekben is eljuttatunk a hozzáférhető, megfelelő működésig.

items.question: Csak auditot is lehet kérni?
items.answer: Igen. Egy WCAG-alapú audit önmagában is értékes kiindulópont: megmutatja a jelenlegi állapotot és a legfontosabb akadályokat. A mi szemléletünkben azonban az audit nem a végállomás, hanem a hozzáférhető szolgáltatás felé vezető út első lépése — a folytatásban is támogatunk, ha igényled.

items.question: Milyen digitális szolgáltatásokat tudtok vizsgálni?
items.answer: Weboldalakat, webshopokat, ügyfélportálokat, mobilalkalmazásokat és belső rendszereket egyaránt. A módszertant mindig az adott termékhez és a vonatkozó előírásokhoz igazítjuk.

items.question: Együtt tudtok dolgozni a fejlesztőcsapatunkkal?
items.answer: Igen, ez sokszor a leghatékonyabb út. A tervezéstől a fejlesztésen át a validációig a projektcsapattal közösen dolgozunk, konkrét, megvalósítható iránymutatással — így az akadálymentesség a napi munka része lesz, nem külön feladat.

items.question: Hogyan zajlik a megfelelőség felé vezető folyamat?
items.answer: Először felmérjük a jelenlegi állapotot, majd priorizált fejlesztési tervet készítünk. Ezt követően közösen javítjuk a megoldást, szükség esetén valódi felhasználókkal validálunk, végül segítünk fenntartható működést és belső képességet kialakítani a jövőbeni fejlesztésekhez.

items.question: Miért több az akadálymentesség, mint jogszabályi megfelelés?
items.answer: A megfelelés a minimum. Az akadálymentesség valójában minőségi kérdés: egy jól hozzáférhető szolgáltatás mindenki számára egyszerűbben használható, több emberhez ér el és erősebb digitális élményt ad. Nálunk ezért nem plusz feladat, hanem a magas minőségű termék egyik alapvető jellemzője.

items.question: Miben más ez, mint egy hagyományos képzés?
items.answer: A hagyományos képzés tudást ad át, majd véget ér. Mi ezzel szemben a szervezet valós projektjein és folyamatain dolgozunk, és a cél nem egy alkalom megtartása, hanem hogy az új szemlélet és módszertan tartósan beépüljön a mindennapi működésbe.

items.question: Kiknek szólnak a programok?
items.answer: Termék-, digitális, UX, Service Design és innovációs csapatoknak, valamint vezetőknek — mindenkinek, aki jobb digitális és AI-alapú döntéseket szeretne hozni. A programot mindig a résztvevők kiindulási szintjéhez és a szervezet céljaihoz igazítjuk.

items.question: Mennyi ideig tart egy program?

items.question: Hogyan biztosítjátok, hogy a megszerzett tudás a napi működés részévé váljon?

items.question: Mi történik a program lezárása után?

content.content: A Works Magyarország egyik vezető UX/UI design és UX research ügynöksége. Hiszünk abban, hogy a jó digitális termékek alapja az emberek mély megértése. Több mint 800 kutatási és 200 design projekt tapasztalatával segítjük ügyfeleinket abban, hogy valódi felhasználói igényekre építsenek.

### Milyen feladatokra számíthatsz?
- Kvalitatív kutatások tervezése és lebonyolítása digitális termékek és szolgáltatások fejlesztéséhez
- Felhasználói interjúk, kérdőíves kutatások és egyéb kutatási módszerek alkalmazása
- Online és offline folyamatok vizsgálata, problémák és fejlesztési lehetőségek feltárása
- Analitikai adatok és felhasználói visszajelzések elemzése
- Kutatási eredmények szintetizálása és prezentálása
- Javaslatok kidolgozása felhasználóközpontú tervezési szemlélet mentén
- Együttműködés designerekkel, fejlesztőkkel, product managerekkel és ügyfelekkel

### Téged keresünk, ha
- Legalább 1 év tapasztalatod van kvalitatív kutatási módszerek gyakorlati alkalmazásában
- Magabiztosan kommunikálsz magyarul és angolul
- Érdekel a digitális termékek és szolgáltatások világa
- Analitikus szemlélettel rendelkezel, és szeretsz összefüggéseket keresni
- Strukturáltan gondolkodsz és képes vagy önállóan dolgozni
- Jó kommunikációs és prezentációs készségekkel rendelkezel
- Szívesen dolgozol csapatban és ügyfelekkel egyaránt

### Előnyt jelent
- UX Research, Service Design, Business Analysis vagy Digital Service Management területen szerzett tapasztalat
- Társadalomtudományi, gazdasági, design vagy egyéb releváns felsőfokú végzettség
- Ismeret usability tesztelésben, workshopok facilitálásában vagy customer journey elemzésben

### Amit kínálunk
- Versenyképes fizetés és juttatási csomag
- Extra szabadnapok az éves szabadságon felül
- Hibrid munkavégzés, heti minimum 2 nap budapesti irodai jelenléttel
- Változatos projektek vezető hazai és nemzetközi vállalatokkal
- Folyamatos szakmai fejlődési lehetőség
- Inspiráló, támogató szakmai közösség
- Laptop, mobiltelefon és mobil előfizetés

projects.title: Alerant Zrt. rebranding
projects.description: One of Hungary’s leading software development companies timed its brand renewal to coincide with its 20th anniversary and an office move. We needed to present a complex service portfolio in a more relaxed, creative style. In addition to redesigning the website, we created the illustrations and creative direction for other digital touchpoints and the wall surfaces of the new office.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: A comprehensive brand identity for a cloud-native technology company

blocks.content: Alerant Zrt. is a major player among Hungarian software development companies. It timed its brand renewal to coincide with its 20th anniversary and an office move. We needed to present a complex service portfolio in a more relaxed, creative style. In addition to redesigning the website, we created the illustrations and creative direction for other digital touchpoints and the wall surfaces of the new office.
The biggest design challenge: how could we translate a technology company’s professional credibility into a distinctive yet approachable visual language?
/strapi/uploads/Alerant_logoanim_1280x896_a84a03f953.gif
blocks.caption: Logo animation

blocks.content: We designed more than a new brand identity: we created a flexible visual system. Three creative concepts and numerous iterations led to the final identity, completed by logo animation, distinctive visual identities for the technology teams, and brand elements carried from digital touchpoints into the offline environment.

seo.metaDescription: A comprehensive rebrand for a Hungarian technology company: brand identity, website and offline visual system from a single source.

projects.title: UNIQA digital self-service
projects.description: Before developing UNIQA’s new digital self-service platform, we used moderated user research to explore how customers think about managing insurance online. The aim was to uncover uncertainties that arise during use and provide the development team with insights to inform design decisions.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: Digital self-service from the user’s perspective for a leading insurer

blocks.content: UNIQA aimed to shift an increasing number of cases from phone and email support to digital self-service channels. Before development began, we set out to understand how well the most important service processes met users’ expectations and where they became uncertain during the process. We used moderated research to examine the entire journey, ensuring development decisions were based on real user behaviour.
The key insight was that users do not get stuck on individual screens; they lose trust when the way the system works differs from their own logic.
/strapi/uploads/UNIQA_ugyfelportal_slide_v2_b18f910b22.png
blocks.caption: Excerpt from the final presentation

blocks.content: Our research revealed how users begin an administrative process, what expectations they bring, and at which points they choose to switch to another channel. The findings informed a wide range of development recommendations that not only improved usability but also helped strengthen trust in digital administration.

seo.metaTitle: UX research for digital insurance self-service | Works.
seo.metaDescription: We used moderated UX research to assess the usability of digital insurance self-service, ensuring development decisions were supported by real user insights.

projects.title: Foundations of accessibility training
projects.description: Through a two-day practical training course, we helped our clients’ specialists carry out accessibility reviews independently, identify the most common WCAG issues and create developer tickets.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: Knowledge that stays with the team long after the project ends

blocks.content: In the long term, accessibility depends not on external audits but on well-prepared in-house teams. Through a two-day practical training course, we shared the knowledge participants needed to carry out accessibility reviews independently, identify issues and create appropriate developer tickets.
The biggest challenge: turning legal and WCAG requirements into practical knowledge that business and product development teams can use every day.
/strapi/uploads/Kepzes_slide_light_115a1f96be.png
blocks.caption: Training curriculum

blocks.content: Alongside the theoretical background, the training placed strong emphasis on practical application. Participants learned to use screen readers, contrast checkers and other testing tools, and practised a complete audit process, from identifying issues to preparing developer documentation. The aim was to enable the organisation to review the accessibility of future developments independently.

seo.metaDescription: Practical WCAG training that equips product and business teams to carry out accessibility reviews independently.

projects.title: Bookline service design

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: Digital experience strategy and product design for Hungary’s largest online bookshop

blocks.content: The project aimed to achieve more than designing a new digital interface. Building on research and business analysis, we developed a vision for an experience ecosystem that gave Bookline a new role in readers’ lives and set a long-term direction for digital development.
The biggest challenge was not designing a new interface, but creating a digital vision that supports both brand positioning and future product development.
/strapi/uploads/Bookline_Home_1_c4e4a45201.png
blocks.caption: Concept design – homepage book recommendations

blocks.content: Over the 18-month collaboration, we shaped the strategic direction through stakeholder interviews, customer research and market benchmarking. UX/UI designs for the digital products were then created based on the experience ecosystem concept, ensuring that strategic thinking and interface design continually reinforced one another.

seo.metaTitle: Digital strategy and UX design for Bookline | Works.
seo.metaDescription: Digital experience strategy, UX research and interface design for Bookline as part of an 18-month strategic project.

projects.title: Funpass Accessibility by Design
projects.description: Before development began, we supplemented the UI designs for Funpass’s new digital service with an accessibility specification. The aim was to embed WCAG 2.1 AA requirements into the product during the design process, minimising the need for later fixes.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: Accessibility begins at the design stage

blocks.content: When designing Funpass’s new digital service, we did not audit a completed interface. Instead, we integrated accessibility considerations as the UI design was being created. We supplemented the Figma designs with detailed professional recommendations so the development team could work to WCAG 2.1 AA guidelines from implementation onwards.
The biggest challenge: integrating accessibility requirements into UI designs in a way that is clear to developers and can be implemented directly.

Rather than setting out requirements in separate documentation, we added accessibility recommendations and best practices directly to the screens in the Figma file. After handing over the documentation, we also provided expert support so the development team could address implementation questions quickly and in line with the standards.

seo.metaDescription: Accessible UI design and WCAG 2.1 AA specifications before development, with Figma-based expert recommendations and developer support.

projects.title: Digital capability building – training
projects.description: We delivered practice-led UX and Service Design training for 10+ organisations, enabling teams to independently develop user-centred digital products and services. Each programme was tailored to the organisation’s ways of working and current challenges.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: Transferring the methodology is just as important as the project itself

blocks.content: Digital product development becomes truly effective when an organisation does not rely solely on external experts, but its own teams also understand the principles of user-centred design. To support this, we developed training programmes that guide participants through the design process, from research to prototyping. Every course was built around practical tasks and real business challenges.
Our aim was not to train UX experts, but to develop business and product teams that can more confidently uncover user problems, make decisions together and design validated solutions.
/strapi/uploads/Design_kepzes_e538e9780d.jpg
blocks.caption: Creative prototyping

blocks.content: The programmes covered research methodology, personas and customer journeys, service blueprints, information architecture, prototyping, user validation and the design sprint mindset. Participants not only learned about the tools but also applied them to their own projects, returning to their day-to-day work with practical methodological knowledge they could use immediately.

seo.metaTitle: Digital capability building and UX training | Works.
seo.metaDescription: Our practice-led UX and Service Design training helps organisations make user-centred digital decisions independently.

projects.title: AI-driven digital product development
projects.description: We developed an AI-driven development methodology that takes an idea to a working, user-validated prototype in just a few weeks. The approach combines AI coding tools, UX research and iterative product development, ensuring that development decisions are informed by real user feedback from the earliest stages.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: From idea to validated prototype in just a few weeks

blocks.content: Számlázz.hu aimed to create AI-based products that could respond quickly to market opportunities while keeping development risk to a minimum. To support this, we developed a new product development operating model built on rapid prototypes, continuous user validation and short iterations instead of traditional, lengthy development cycles. The methodology aimed not only to create new products, but also to establish an AI-native development mindset that could be applied across the organisation.

The focus of development was not on delivering the final product as quickly as possible, but on accelerating learning. With AI, the team created working prototypes within a few weeks and validated them with real users, enabling development decisions to be based on evidence rather than assumptions.
/strapi/uploads/Alerant_logoanim_1280x896_a84a03f953.gif
blocks.caption: Logo animation

blocks.content: The operating model established during the pilot begins with stakeholder interviews and use-case prioritisation, followed by rapid prototyping using AI-driven development. These prototypes are then supported by ongoing user research and validation. With predefined decision points, the governance model ensures that every next step is linked to business goals and user feedback. The result is a repeatable development process that significantly reduces risk and shortens the path from idea to market.

seo.metaTitle: AI prototyping and digital product development | Works.
seo.metaDescription: Our AI-driven product development methodology takes ideas to working, user-validated prototypes in just a few weeks.

projects.title: UniCredit accessibility audit
projects.description: We carried out an accessibility audit of UniCredit Bank's mobile banking app and online banking platform in line with WCAG 2.1 AA guidelines. The project aimed to ensure the digital services met the accessibility requirements coming into force in 2025, while delivering an easier-to-use experience for everyone.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: Making digital banking accessible to everyone

blocks.content: We carried out an accessibility audit of UniCredit Bank's mobile banking app and online banking platform against the WCAG 2.1 AA standard. We assessed more than thirty user journeys across iOS, Android and web environments to identify the functional barriers that make banking services harder to use for customers relying on assistive technology.
The biggest challenge was assessing the accessibility of a highly complex mobile banking ecosystem in a way that made the identified issues clearly actionable for developers.
/strapi/uploads/image_1785160439920_af0ef5ac33.png
blocks.caption: Accessibility – service overview

blocks.content: During the audit, we not only identified accessibility gaps but also prepared development recommendations for every issue. We used screen readers, contrast checkers and other assistive technologies, then delivered the findings in a severity-prioritised report that directly supported the development team’s work. The project also included expert consultation, enabling us to find solutions together for questions arising during implementation.

seo.metaTitle: UniCredit mobile banking accessibility audit | Works.
seo.metaDescription: WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility audit for mobile and online banking, with development recommendations and expert support.

projects.title: Rudas Thermal Baths service design
projects.description: We examined the end-to-end guest experience at Rudas Thermal Baths using research and service design methods. The aim was to create an operating model that improves the guest experience, supports employees and preserves the baths’ historic character.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: Rethinking the guest experience through research, service design and operational development

blocks.content: The project was not about developing a digital interface, but about rethinking the entire guest experience. Through qualitative and quantitative research, stakeholder interviews, ethnographic observation, social listening and service safari methodology, we uncovered the needs of different guest groups, then translated these insights into personas and customer journeys.
We turned research findings directly into operational development decisions: from personas and customer journeys through to the future service blueprint.
/strapi/uploads/Rudas_asszociacios_kartyak_fcfa1ab918.png
blocks.caption: Association cards for on-site interviews

blocks.content: Rudas presented a particular challenge: we had to account simultaneously for its historical heritage and the differing expectations of regular local visitors, tourists and therapeutic guests. By the end of the project, we had produced a prioritised development roadmap to support implementation, from quick interventions to longer-term directions for service and operational development.

seo.metaTitle: Rudas Baths: service design and guest experience | Works.
seo.metaDescription: Service design for Rudas Thermal Baths: research, stakeholder interviews, customer journeys, personas and a service blueprint to improve the guest experience.

projects.title: AI-powered categorisation of Google Maps reviews
projects.description: We processed thousands of Google Maps reviews using artificial intelligence to provide a structured view of the customer experience. AI not only categorised the reviews, but also identified recurring themes, pain points and opportunities for improvement, turning free-text feedback into directly actionable decision-support insights.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: Structured insights from thousands of customer reviews in a short time
caseStudy.client: K&H Bank, Budapest Gyógyfürdői és Hévizei

blocks.content: Google Maps reviews contain highly valuable customer feedback, but their volume makes manual processing slow and difficult to scale. We developed an AI-based analysis process that automatically processes free-text reviews, identifies the key themes, groups recurring issues and organises the results into a consistent structure.

We did not increase the number of reviews; we made them easier to interpret. In just a few hours, AI provided an overall picture of thousands of reviews that would have taken days or weeks to process manually.
/strapi/uploads/Google_maps_a4ea8c4535.png
blocks.caption: Google reviews analysis – excerpt from the final presentation

blocks.content: The outcome was not a simple sentiment analysis, but a decision-support insight system. AI identified the most frequent positive and negative themes, uncovered recurring pain points, and enabled results to be filtered by location, topic or customer need. This turned free-text feedback into directly actionable input for service development and customer experience decisions.

seo.metaTitle: AI-powered Google Maps review analysis | Works.
seo.metaDescription: We used AI to process thousands of Google Maps reviews, uncovering structured insights and opportunities to improve the customer experience.

projects.title: Establishing AI-based research
projects.description: We developed an AI-based way of working for Magyar Telekom’s research team that makes secondary analysis of qualitative research faster, more consistent and independently repeatable. The project was not about teaching an AI tool, but about how artificial intelligence can be integrated safely and reliably into research processes.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: We did not train AI; we established a new way of working in research.

blocks.content: Telekom researchers work with large volumes of interview material every day, but producing secondary analyses required considerable manual effort. The goal was not simply to demonstrate the use of AI, but to establish an operating model that accounted for corporate data security requirements, research quality expectations and the available technology environment. To achieve this, we adapted the capabilities, limitations and potential applications of existing AI tools to Telekom’s own research processes.

The outcome of the project was not training material, but a repeatable way of working. The research team learned how to produce faster, more reliable AI-supported secondary analyses without compromising research quality or data security.
/strapi/uploads/AI_tamogatott_kutatas_3cb6dd6087.png
blocks.caption: AI-supported research process

blocks.content: As part of the programme, we tested the LLMs used by Telekom alongside other research-support platforms, compared their outputs with previous human analyses, and developed the recommended prompting and validation methodology. The training was followed by a workshop, enabling the team to apply the new way of working confidently in their own projects.

seo.metaTitle: AI capability building for research teams | Works.
seo.metaDescription: We help research teams integrate AI safely and effectively into qualitative research, from secondary analysis to day-to-day operations.

projects.title: ONE - Digital identification
projects.description: We underpinned the redesign of One’s customer identification process with qualitative and quantitative research. The project aimed to create a simpler sign-in experience while exploring the user and business requirements for introducing two-step verification.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: User research to rethink the identification experience for a customer base of several million

blocks.content: Following the integration of DIGI and Vodafone, One’s customer identification process became complex. The aim of the research was not only to examine the usability of the current login process, but also to understand users’ expectations, their attitudes towards different identification methods, and the conditions under which they would accept two-factor authentication. Qualitative usability testing was complemented by quantitative research, allowing decisions to be based on real user behaviour and large-sample data.

The research’s key finding was that users do not reject two-factor authentication; they reject unnecessary friction. They accept security steps when they appear in a context they understand and protect something of real value.
/strapi/uploads/Azonositasi_modok_kedveltsege_slide_b7266baf7c.png
blocks.caption: Quantitative survey results – excerpt from the final presentation

blocks.content: The research uncovered the prototype’s key usability issues, critical drop-off points in the login process, and user attitudes towards different identification methods. The findings directly supported the design of the new login process and the rollout strategy for two-factor authentication, while helping to balance security and user experience.

seo.metaTitle: UX research for One’s identification process | Works.
seo.metaDescription: We helped redesign One’s customer identification and introduce two-step verification through qualitative and quantitative UX research.

projects.title: Yettel - AI-based IVR validation
projects.description: We reimagined the traditional tree test with a proprietary AI simulator. The solution enabled 80 users to try a total of 40 different service scenarios in a realistic environment, quickly and at scale.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: We validated the usability of a complex IVR menu system with a proprietary AI simulator.

blocks.content: Before redesigning a complex IVR menu system, the client wanted to understand whether customers would be able to find the service path relevant to them within the revised menu structure. Rather than using conventional research methods, we developed a proprietary AI-powered simulator that modelled realistic telephone service scenarios and enabled rapid validation with a large sample.
With 80 users, 40 service scenarios and hundreds of simulated paths, we validated the entire IVR structure in just a few weeks.
/strapi/uploads/Yettel_b6d6aecb20.png
blocks.caption: Questionnaire

blocks.content: Through a web interface, testers logged into their own profiles and completed randomly assigned service tasks. The system recorded not only whether they found the right menu item, but also the paths they took, incorrect decisions, backtracking, and users’ confidence and perceived difficulty. We analysed the results using heatmaps and detailed path analyses, making it possible to identify precisely which menu items needed redesigning.

seo.metaTitle: AI-based IVR validation with a proprietary simulator | Works
seo.metaDescription: We validated a complex IVR menu with our AI simulator. Tests with 80 users across 40 service scenarios informed development decisions.

projects.title: Chefparade service design
projects.description: For Chefparade, we identified what was preventing guests from returning and developed a new customer experience and communications strategy based on the research findings.

caseStudy.heroSubtitle: Increasing returning guest numbers through research

blocks.content: Although Chefparade’s courses achieved exceptionally high satisfaction ratings, most guests returned only once or twice. The project aimed to understand where the customer relationship breaks down and which experiential or operational factors would encourage more regular attendance. To do so, we conducted competitor analysis, data analysis, stakeholder and customer interviews, a website audit, and a questionnaire survey involving 1,440 respondents.

The research’s most important insight was that the issue lay not in the quality of the experience, but in the continuity of the guest relationship. After the first course, there was no deliberate approach to building the experience and relationship that could have fostered long-term engagement.
/strapi/uploads/Tanulo_slide_b46bdc21f1.png
blocks.caption: Persona card

blocks.content: During the research, we developed a motivation-based rather than demographic segmentation. We found that guests come for the same service for very different reasons: some want to learn, while others are primarily looking for a shared experience. By mapping the full customer journey, we identified pain points and opportunities for improvement at every touchpoint, then turned these into a strategic roadmap for communications, the digital experience, the loyalty programme and service development.

blogPosts.title: Should we entrust AI with analysing user feedback?
blogPosts.excerpt: We compared the results of four AI models and three human analysts while labelling 100 user feedback entries.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Bízzuk az AI-ra a felhasználói visszajelzések elemzését?

content.content: ### We compared the results of four language models with human analyses
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_bizzuk_az_ai_ra_a_felhasznaloi_visszajelzesek_elemzeset_1_7e4328d31a.png

Users constantly talk about services, apps and products: in Google reviews, app stores, forums, on social media and even through customer service channels. These are not responses to questionnaires, but voluntary, spontaneous opinions. That makes them highly valuable data, but also noisy. To use them for product or service development decisions, it is worth structuring this organic feedback in some way.

**The challenge, then, is not a lack of data, but interpreting it.**

What are people actually talking about? What themes, complaints and development needs emerge from the texts? The clearest answers come from identifying patterns in the feedback, then labelling and categorising the texts accordingly. Small volumes of data can be processed effectively by people, but when volumes are large and analysis is ongoing, an appealing question arises: can we entrust the work to a language model? And if so, which one, how should we use it, and what pitfalls should we expect? We explored these questions through user reviews of a banking mobile app.

### Method

We asked four language models (GPT/ChatGPT, Sonnet/Claude, RoBERTa and LLaMA) and three people to label 100 user feedback entries according to predefined categories. We had the language models perform the same task three times. This allowed us to examine not only how closely AI solutions resembled human reasoning, but also the models’ consistency (in other words, whether individual models could reproduce their own results).

ChatGPT and Claude performed the labelling task based on a prompt; we used the RoBERTa and LLaMA models via the [NLP Cloud](https://nlpcloud.com) categorisation platform, while the human participants received written instructions.

**NLP Cloud**

NLP Cloud is an online platform that makes a range of artificial intelligence models available both through its website and via an API. It offers tools for several types of task, including a module for text categorisation. Through this, we controlled the RoBERTa and LLaMA models (unlike Claude and ChatGPT) not with textual instructions, but programmatically via an API.
We iterated once on the prompts for ChatGPT and Claude, so these models carried out the labelling in two rounds, 2*3 times in total (see Table 1).
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_bizzuk_az_ai_ra_a_felhasznaloi_visszajelzesek_elemzeset_2_e55fdf6727.png
content.caption: Table 1: Models used and types of instruction
content.alt: 1. táblázat: Használt modellek és instrukciók típusa

content.content:
### Lesson 1: the importance of how instructions are phrased

In the first round, ChatGPT achieved 100% consistency, meaning it produced exactly the same result in all three runs. At first glance, this seemed like an excellent result, but it was actually so stable for the wrong reason: the model fell into anchoring bias, assigning virtually everything to the same single category, regardless of the content of the texts.

With the same prompt, Claude performed as we expected. It used several categories, and its results matched across the three runs 83% of the time.

**Anchoring bias**

The phenomenon in which the first piece of information received (the “anchor”) disproportionately influences subsequent judgements and decisions, even when the anchor is partly or entirely irrelevant. (For further examples and research on anchoring bias in AI, see [this link](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214635024000868).)

We then refined the prompt and ran it three times with both models. In this second round, ChatGPT became anchored in only one run, while the other two produced more varied labelling. As a result, however, the three runs differed substantially, leaving ChatGPT with 10% consistency in this round. This is unacceptable for structured, repeatable analytical tasks.

For Claude, the refined prompt reduced stability: consistency fell from 83% to 63% (see Table 2). This also shows that different models may respond differently to the same prompt and the same modification.

We did not run LLaMA and RoBERTa using textual prompts, but through a solution designed specifically for text categorisation, using Python code. Here, LLaMA showed 95% consistency and RoBERTa 100% consistency.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_bizzuk_az_ai_ra_a_felhasznaloi_visszajelzesek_elemzeset_3_8205479cbf.png
content.caption: Table 2: Model consistency based on three runs
content.alt: 2.táblázat: Modellek konzisztenciája három futtatás alapján

content.content:
The consistency of results is greatly influenced by how we run the task and the constraints we set around it. Chat-based generative models (ChatGPT, Claude) are more sensitive to small differences in wording, so the same task can produce different labels across multiple runs. Although LLaMA is also a generative model, like the models behind ChatGPT and Claude, we ran it in a structured way (via a categorisation API, using code and a fixed set of labels), which gave us much more stable results. RoBERTa works on a different principle from the other three models and is specifically optimised for classification. As such, 100% consistency is to be expected from this model.

### Lesson 2: consistency ≠ quality

For ChatGPT, perfect consistency concealed false results. By contrast, RoBERTa was 100% stable while using a range of labels, as expected. However, when we compared RoBERTa’s solution with the results of human labelling (using the consensus labels of the three participants), the two matched only 25% of the time.

**So RoBERTa was stable, but its solution differed substantially from human reasoning.**

### Lesson 3: people do not always agree with one another either

Before expecting AI models to provide consistent solutions that also make sense to us, it is worth looking at how people perform on the same labelling task. Three assessors worked independently on the same 100 user feedback entries, using the same 10 predefined labels.

We compared the three participants’ solutions pairwise and found that they matched 44%, 46% and 58% of the time, respectively (see Figure 1). There was complete agreement (where all three participants chose the same label) for one-third of the texts, while there was complete disagreement (where three different labels were assigned) in 20% of cases.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_bizzuk_az_ai_ra_a_felhasznaloi_visszajelzesek_elemzeset_4_4443059c6d.png
content.caption: Figure 1: Overlap between the solutions of the three assessors
content.alt: 1. ábra: A három értékelő személy megoldása közötti átfedések

content.content:
This is not a sign of carelessness, but a question of the precision and clarity of the labels. It is not only the names of the labels that matter, but also how many labels apply to a given text. If several labels fit a text but only one can be selected, that does not support a clear decision. The precision and clarity of the category system is a key issue for both people and AI.

**Where people’s decisions differ, we cannot expect AI to give a uniform answer either.**

### Summary of results
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_bizzuk_az_ai_ra_a_felhasznaloi_visszajelzesek_elemzeset_5_1da2cdf82d.png
content.caption: Figure 2: Consistency and quality of the solutions produced by the models studied (relative to the human solution)
content.alt: 2. ábra: A vizsgált modellek megoldásainak konzisztenciája és minősége (az emberi megoldáshoz viszonyítva)

content.content:
Of the four models, LLaMA offered the best balance of consistency and quality: it was 95% consistent, and its solution matched human labelling 63% of the time (see Figure 2). Claude’s solution also matched that of the human participants 63% of the time, but this model was less consistent (63%).

It may seem low that the AI solutions matched those of humans at most 63% of the time. However, the human participants did not think alike either: during labelling, they reached the same decision at most 58% of the time.

**In this light, AI–human agreement of around 60% is not weak performance, but an approximation of the level of agreement between different ways of human thinking.**

### What does this mean in practice?

It does not mean that AI is unreliable, nor does it mean that it replaces people. Rather, it means we need to ask the question differently: not “Which AI is best?”, but “Which model is suitable for which task, under what conditions?”

1. If large volumes need to be processed automatically, LLaMA in structured mode is the most balanced choice.
2. If we want a quick, exploratory analysis and the results will be reviewed by a person, Claude or ChatGPT can also do the job. In this case, careful prompt development and testing are essential.
3. If the category system is well defined, RoBERTa may be the best solution after fine-tuning.

Content labelling is not merely a technological question; it is also a task of interpretation. Model performance can only be properly understood in the context of the quality of the category system, the task definition and human context.

**Even at its best, AI does not deliver absolute truth; it approximates human consensus.**
Author: Zsuzsa Székely, Experience Designer at Works.

blogPosts.title: Where is the design profession heading? Customer-centred thinking in an AI-accelerated world – Part 2
blogPosts.excerpt: In digital product development, professional execution is no longer a distinctive competitive advantage: in the age of AI, high-quality implementation has become readily accessible to everyone. This shift has brought fundamental dilemmas around professional roles to the surface, where the real opportunity lies not in the speed of execution but in the ability to interpret strategically and connect the dots.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Merre tart a design szakma, az ügyfélközpontú gondolkozás egy AI-val gyorsított világban? – 2. rész

content.content:
### When execution no longer sets you apart

Democratisation, role tensions and the real point of differentiation
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_amikor_a_kivitelezes_mar_nem_kulonboztet_meg_1_105bfc5ede.png
content.caption: Looking beyond execution: the paper boats represent generic solutions available to anyone. The beam reaching into the depths is strategic interpretation, revealing the system’s real connections beyond technical implementation.
content.alt: Látni a kivitelezés mögé: A papírhajók a bárki által elérhető tucatmegoldások. A mélybe hatoló fénysugár a stratégiai értelmezés, amely a technikai megvalósításon túl a rendszer valódi összefüggéseit tárja fel.

content.content:
### 4. AI and the democratisation of design

One of AI’s most tangible effects on design is the democratisation of execution. Tasks that previously required specialist knowledge can now be completed quickly and with a low barrier to entry. Layouts, UI structures, microcopy and simple flows can now be produced to an “good enough” standard.

This is not inherently a problem. The tension arises because **understanding the consequences is not democratised alongside execution**. An “good enough” solution may work technically while taking the system in the wrong direction.

### 5. The mid-level–senior tension: not a generational issue, but a question of roles

Democratisation makes it clear what being senior really means today. For a long time, superior execution was the differentiating value. But that advantage disappears when the technical part of execution is no longer a bottleneck.

The tension does not arise between mid-level and senior professionals, but within the “senior” category itself. Those who can frame, prioritise and foresee the consequences of decisions remain relevant. Here, democratisation does not destroy – it creates selection.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_amikor_a_kivitelezes_mar_nem_kulonboztet_meg_2_971c808b5d.png

### 6. Not a lack of data, but a lack of interpretation

Today, data is rarely what is missing. More often, it is the ability to form the available signals into a meaningful whole. Insights come from different channels, relate to different timeframes, and often contradict one another.

This does not create a lack of decisions, but **interpretative overload**. More and more decisions extend beyond the boundaries of a single team or project, yet we do not always see this in advance. The greatest risk is often not a poor solution, but the wrong focus.

### 7. The point of differentiation: interpretation, not execution

In this environment, design’s real point of differentiation is not execution. Value is created where someone can connect signals, prioritise problems and put decisions into context.

This is not a conventional UX task, nor is it a new methodology. It is a shift in perspective: recognising that not all data is equally valuable, not every insight requires an immediate response, and not every “good enough” solution takes us in the right direction.

Design is increasingly faced with a choice. It can remain a supporting function within a more complex system – or embrace the role of helping to interpret what is really happening. Looking towards 2026, to me this is not a technological question, but a professional decision.
[Part one: When design starts searching for its place again](/blog/amikor-a-design-ujra-keresi-a-helyet)
The author is Ákos Maczinkó, Managing Director of Works.

blogPosts.title: Where is the design profession and customer-centred thinking heading in an AI-accelerated world? – Part 1
blogPosts.excerpt: The world of digital products has changed considerably, and familiar design methods alone no longer always provide answers to today’s more complex challenges. The arrival of AI has brought questions about how companies operate to the surface – questions that previously received little attention.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Merre tart a design szakma, az ügyfélközpontú gondolkozás egy AI-val gyorsított világban? – 1. rész

content.content:
### When design is finding its place again

Thoughts on design roles, AI and customer-centred ways of working at the beginning of 2026
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_amikor_a_design_ujra_keresi_a_helyet_1_aa67e1f3f8.png
content.caption: Order in chaos: the fog represents the information, opinions and uncertainty in which we often lose our way. The glowing crystal is design itself: the moment confused ideas become a solid decision to build on.
content.alt: Rend a káoszban : A köd a rengeteg infót, véleményt és bizonytalanságot mutatja, amiben sokszor elveszünk. A középen ragyogó kristály maga a design: az a pillanat, amikor a sok zavaros ötletből végre összeáll egy szilárd döntés, amire lehet építeni.

content.content:
### Introduction

I have worked in and around customer-centred design for more than fifteen years. I have seen UX and CX evolve from a niche, long-marginal approach into a core principle of digital operations. Research, testing, workshops, journeys – these have all become everyday tools, and we rarely need to explain why the customer perspective matters.

And yet, lately I have increasingly felt that we have stalled.

Not because UX does not work. Quite the opposite: the methods are more mature, faster and more accessible than ever. The question is whether **the same answers we learnt in a simpler environment are enough for today’s more complex operational challenges**.

This is not a list of trends. Rather, it is an analytical reflection on how the role of design is changing in a more complex, uncertain environment – and why this has once again become a relevant question.

### 1. Design searching for its role in a more mature environment

Design is now present almost everywhere. It is part of product development, it appears in organisational language, and its legitimacy rarely needs to be justified. Yet in many organisations, its role remains difficult to define.

If someone works in sales, IT or marketing, it is generally clear what that means: which decisions they influence and what they are responsible for. With design, this is far less clear. The same job title can represent very different roles in different places.

This partly stems from the nature of design: it is a cross-disciplinary profession that brings together business, technology and customer perspectives. The problem arises when this position at the intersection **is not a conscious decision but an established practice**: design is ‘there’, it is involved, but it is unclear when and on which issues it carries real weight. In such cases, design can easily remain a support function: helping to make the case, make decisions easier to understand and reduce friction – but rarely shaping direction. For a long time, this was not critical. Digital products used to be simpler, appeared across fewer channels, and the impact of decisions often remained within the boundaries of an individual team or function. 
Today, the digital experience is created across multiple channels through the collaboration of several teams and systems, while customers’ expectations and sensitivity have also increased. 
What is more, an increasing number of decisions extend beyond a single project or organisational unit. In this environment, a purely supportive role for design is no longer enough. Not because design wants more, but because **the environment places greater weight on the questions** it has traditionally addressed: connections, consequences and operations understood from the customer’s perspective.

### 2. AI is not a tool, but an operational catalyst

We often talk about AI as a new tool or feature. In reality, however, it rarely remains within the boundaries of a single team or system. As soon as it appears, it brings questions to the surface that often had not even been considered before: who can use it, what decisions it can make, who is accountable, and how it fits into the overall operation.

These questions affect the business, IT, legal, customer service and customer experience teams at the same time. AI is therefore not a technological issue, but an **operational issue**. It is a catalyst: it amplifies organisational tensions that were previously less visible.

This is where the **service design** perspective becomes especially relevant. Not as a methodology, but as a framework for thinking: one that connects different perspectives and makes the consequences of decisions explicit.

### 3. Experimentation as a responsible implementation model

An AI implementation is expensive, uncertain and difficult to reverse – both technologically and organisationally. The ‘big bang’ approach is therefore particularly risky. Instead, **experimentation**, and particularly the **POC (Proof of Concept) as a learning methodology**, is increasingly coming to the fore.

Here, a POC is not a technology demo, but the validation of a hypothesis: whether AI provides a genuinely meaningful answer to a specific operational problem. Validation is not only technical, but also organisational, legal and customer-focused. The aim is not rapid implementation, but learning and building buy-in.

This approach clearly shows that design – particularly in the service design sense – does not accelerate; it provides a framework. It helps ensure that experimentation is not an ad hoc attempt, but a deliberate path to implementation.
[Part two: When execution no longer sets you apart](/en/blog/when-execution-no-longer-sets-you-apart)
The author is Ákos Maczinkó, Managing Director of Works.

blogPosts.title: Can AI take my job?
blogPosts.excerpt: At the start of 2026, qualitative research is no longer about tedious note-taking and endless searching. We show how AI becomes a researcher’s ‘superpower’, from transcription to benchmark analysis, and why expert context-setting makes human involvement irreplaceable.

content.content:
### The role of AI in processing qualitative research

Some professionals have wondered whether the arrival of AI in research could lead to the full automation of research. After all, LLM-based tools are advancing month by month, or even week by week. By now, they are not only capable of summarising, identifying patterns or carrying out comprehensive analysis; they can even take over moderating conversations from the researcher. This raises the question of whether there will be any research tasks left for humans to carry out in the future.

However, as another group of researchers gain more experience with LLM software and AI-supported research platforms, they are seeing more clearly what these tools can help with and how they can make work more efficient. They are also seeing more clearly what their limitations are, and which questions and topics cannot be meaningfully answered without human involvement.

Yet another group of professionals is becoming increasingly convinced that we need not worry: research will not become automated. Instead, it will become more valuable, as AI becomes increasingly able to support this work too. It is also becoming ever clearer that the work can only be complete with us, the researchers; only our expertise can deliver truly good results. This is also the position we take here at Works.

In this article, I focus on presenting the benefits of using artificial intelligence during the analysis phase of research.

We have always sought to respond to our clients’ needs with the greatest possible care. After all, if they are satisfied, trust us and receive the right support from us in resolving their business dilemmas, they will turn to us again next time.

Our experimentation with AI is also driven by client needs. I will show which effective, machine-supported solutions appear to be delivering results at present, in January 2026.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_elveheti_az_ai_a_munkamat_1_4f8b0ffaf7.png
content.caption: Research as shared construction: solid human foundations and a guiding ‘blueprint’ (context) are essential, while AI rapidly puts complex data blocks in place to build knowledge. (The symbolic concept and image were created by Gemi...
content.alt: A kutatás mint közös építkezés: a biztos humán alapok és az irányt mutató „tervrajz” (a kontextus) nélkülözhetetlenek, miközben az AI a nehéz adatblokkok villámgyors helyretételében segít felépíteni a tudást. (A szimbolikus koncepciót és a képet a Gemini alkotta meg.)

content.content:
### Client need #1: I want the results by next week, too!

### Accurate transcripts, quickly

The most time-consuming step in qualitative research is producing suitable transcripts and notes from interviews. We know — and many of us find it hard to accept — that there is only one way to do this: taking detailed notes while listening back to the interviews. This often takes two or three times as long as the interview itself. After that, all the remaining steps are shorter and more enjoyable: examining patterns, identifying and categorising problems, understanding causes and effects, formulating recommendations and preparing the presentation.

We have been planning to automate the least-loved step mentioned above for a long time. We use Teams to conduct interviews, and quickly realised that although it does produce a transcript, it unfortunately requires a great deal of human correction before we can use it effectively for synthesis and analysis. Since the rise of generative AI, we have therefore been exploring tools designed to produce accurate transcripts, and last year we finally found one or more that provide suitable quality in Hungarian too. Comparing them is made possible by a method called WER — Word Error Rate — which involves counting misunderstood, omitted and incorrectly inserted words, then dividing their total by the number of correctly identified words. We achieved a rate below 15% with these tools, which is considered a particularly good result, whereas Teams produced results between 50% and 60%.

So, with minimal human time investment, we can have an excellent transcript. We can save a great deal of time at this stage with [Transkriptor](https://transkriptor.com/app/signin/) or [Turboscribe](https://turboscribe.ai/hu).

### Finding quotes no longer takes hours in the final push to produce a presentation

There is another step that is fairly slow and, on a rushed project, sometimes gets left out altogether: adding suitable quotes to the presentation for each insight. You might think accurate transcripts make these easier to find again, but in reality they do not. The moderator will certainly remember which participant expressed an idea that strongly supports our point, but locating it in a 30–40-page transcript — and knowing exactly what phrase to ‘Ctrl+F’ — is more difficult. NotebookLM has sped up this step for us. When asked the right questions about the transcripts, it immediately produces the relevant quotes without hallucinating, as it only works with the uploaded texts.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_elveheti_az_ai_a_munkamat_2_f6192a46ec.png
content.caption: A tool for clarity: AI can act like a prism, breaking down the incoming chaotic mass of raw data into clear, interpretable insight patterns, but it needs a human hand to hold and focus it at the right angle. (The symbolic concept and the ...
content.alt: A tisztánlátás eszköze: az AI prizmaként képes a beérkező kaotikus, nyers adathalmazt tiszta, értelmezhető insight-mintázatokká bontani, de szükség van az emberi kézre, amely a megfelelő szögben tartja és fókuszálja azt. (A szimbolikus koncepciót és a képet a Gemini alkotta meg.)

content.content:
### Client need #2: I want even higher-quality results!

To assess how AI can deliver on this, we have introduced a new experimental way of working. Once the transcripts are ready, the research team splits into two: one group analyses them in the traditional way, while the other uses various AI tools. This is the only way to judge the quality of support AI can provide.

Let’s look at how the AI-supported team works:

They use LLM-based chatbots, which can provide valuable support for thinking and analysis when used well. The key is prompting and providing context.

### Effective prompting and context-setting are essential

When talking to AI chatbots, establish the context too: provide the business objective, research objective and hypotheses, then begin the conversation. After all, if your ‘conversation partner’ does not understand the parameters, it will not be able to help appropriately.

Use effective prompts: be specific, define the research questions or the sub-questions whose answers can move you towards the results in the right direction. For example, do not ask it to summarise the conversation, nor ask which participant highlighted what when using a given feature. Instead, ask what similarities and differences emerged in each participant’s thoughts about that feature.
