It is also worth adding details based on your own interview experience: for example, ask it to separate thoughts about the service from those about usability, or to focus exclusively on the analytical considerations needed for the given project.

And who could be better at prompting and setting context than a qualitative researcher?

For us, prompting and creating context did not enter our lives with AI. In every qualitative methodology where flexibility is necessary for good results, and paying attention to our conversation partner may raise new questions at any time, we need to ask those questions. At the right time, with the right question. So we prompt regularly in our interviews, and this knowledge has been highly useful in conversations with AI chatbots.

In research, the context we provide at the beginning of most conversations with participants is of particular importance. If it is not right, the participant may approach, for example, their understanding of a prototype concept from a completely different perspective. For instance, if we use dummy prices in a prototype while testing a purchasing journey, it is vital to clarify the parameters for the participant in advance, so they can focus on ergonomics rather than the prices.

Researchers consciously develop their ability to prompt and set context in their early years, before it becomes instinctive. These are the skills we need to apply when using generative AI-based tools.

Some tools immediately suggest a new approach or next step. Do not let a good suggestion carry you away in the conversation. Just make a note of it, but first work through the questions according to your own approach. It is important that when asking questions, just as when we interview participants, we do not lead the machine either. Do not ask it to compile difficulties and problems, because then that is what it will generate, amplifying things that human analysis would not.

### Using research platforms

Companies have long had access to numerous research-support platforms that could already provide good support for human analysis. However, over the past two years, almost all of them have added some kind of AI-supported feature, while new platforms promising near-miraculous results have also emerged. Naturally, we continue to experiment with these too, because comparing them lets us see where each one excels and how it can properly support our or our clients’ day-to-day work.

Over recent months, I have been able to group the platforms we reviewed and tried as follows. What they had in common: a great landing page that makes you want to start using them, but… There is always a but; in this case, the following:

- But the platform does not properly support qualitative research, instead enabling other types of voice-of-customer processing. These include Kraftful, Collectif, Notably, Attention Insight
- But it is only available after an online demo. For example: Yabble, Dovetail.
- But it does not speak Hungarian, like Askviable, Innerview or Viable.

And after all this, a few platforms remained that we could genuinely start using, and have enjoyed working with ever since, where the project allows.

### Doreveal

It not only supports human analysis with tagging, organising by tags, and the ability to highlight quotations from transcripts and videos; after video files are uploaded, it can also summarise the key statements from each interview according to the research questions, answering the relevant question in each case. With one click, I can access the related video or transcript excerpts. This provides substantial support and a quick overview during the first stages of synthesis. In other words, there is no need for a transcript: it can already generate findings from the video file itself. Hungarian remains a challenge with this software, because although it can accept Hungarian-language inputs (briefs, guides, interviews and research questions), it gives its responses in English whenever we ask for help. This does require some compromise, but otherwise it supports us like a good research partner.

### Marvin

For a long time, this platform did not speak Hungarian either, but it can now support the work as a fully fledged research partner. What is particularly useful is that it not only summarises according to the research questions provided in advance, but can also answer specific questions, with references to the relevant interviews. Not only is an AI summary automatically generated for each interview, but AI notes can also be requested. This can be an enormous help if anyone outside the research team, from the business team or management, wants to gain an insight. If a team member can devote an hour to the research, this feature is more useful than listening to just one interview, as it can provide a far more complete picture of participants’ experiences.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_elveheti_az_ai_a_munkamat_3_2f4cf2e577.png
content.caption: Navigating the unknown: AI rapidly maps the ‘digital terrain’ of an ever-changing market, but human expertise sets the goal and finds the right direction through the noise. (The symbolic concept and image were created by Gemini ...
content.alt: Navigáció az ismeretlenben: a folyton változó piaci környezet „digitális terepasztalát” az AI segít villámgyorsan feltérképezni, de a célt és a helyes irányt a humán szakértelem jelöli ki a zajban. (A szimbolikus koncepciót és a képet a Gemini alkotta meg.)

content.content:
### Client need #3: Could you understand us even better?

Based on feedback from most of our clients, we can say that clients like working with us because we understand them, their industry and their problems well, and can formulate commercially relevant recommendations to help them develop further. But this can always be done even better.

### Market context

Even if our domain knowledge is strong, changes in regulation or competitors’ activities may not immediately come into view. In this area too, asking an AI chatbot for help is useful. In such cases, there is no need to ask our client to establish the current market situation; we can simply ask the machine, and only consult the client if something still remains unclear.

### Benchmark analyses

It has never been this easy. Of course, with persistent searching we could previously find the services and websites that could be reviewed as benchmarks or best practices: examples to follow or avoid. But a typical problem was that finding these solutions, especially international ones, took far more time than finding participants who used them. And it was easy enough for those participants to show us in detail the solution we ourselves saw as a good example.

Generative AI can now review pages it considers relevant much sooner and list them for us. Naturally, we experts still need to verify them in the familiar way afterwards. It can save days.

### Previous research and publications

We often encounter a new product, service or feature idea for which we do not have adequate information about potential users’ needs, and the project’s scope does not allow us — whether in time or budget — to establish through research whether the direction is genuinely right. As with benchmark analyses, we could previously search for these using Google, but finding relevant information in these searches was perhaps even harder than simply looking for a service or product. Today, however, we have access to an AI-supported solution that searches only research and publications considered sound by experts too (peer-reviewed), and provides useful results for any question, along with a short summary and access to the full document. Even for a completely new product idea, feel free to turn to it and ask whether it can find any research material on the subject. If it can, you will gain information that only a few years ago might have required research costing millions of forints. [It would be a mistake to miss it!](https://consensus.app/)

### Change is the only constant

At the beginning of 2026, we see these as the client needs for which artificial intelligence supports us as a valuable partner. Week by week, however, we see how much more people are able to get out of AI, how significantly the tools are developing, and how they enable us to develop too. This year, we will continue working to keep pace with the development of these tools.

We still cannot clearly see everything we will be able to use it for in the future, nor what it will not be suitable for, however hard we try. But we are following these opportunities closely, and will continue to share our knowledge and experience with you regularly.
This article was written by Bartha Gizella, Senior Experience Designer at Works.

blogPosts.title: From new starter to colleague
blogPosts.excerpt: A new person joining always stirs things up a little — in the best possible way. They bring fresh ideas and new perspectives which, in an organisation of 20–25 people, can have an impact on the whole company without exaggeration. It is the organisation’s responsibility to ensure that this new energy is integrated, while individuality and character are retained.

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_uj_belepobol_kollega_1_e847a224ef.png

### How we welcome new arrivals at Works.

A new person joining always stirs things up a little — in the best possible way. They bring fresh ideas and new perspectives which, in an organisation of 20–25 people, can have an impact on the whole company without exaggeration. It is our responsibility to ensure that this new energy is integrated, while individuality and character are retained. We believe this can be achieved with sufficient attention, though making it happen in day-to-day practice is not always without its challenges.

### The first 100 days

At Works., every new starter goes through the steps of the ‘First 100 Days’. This is not a political programme or a catchy HR slogan, but a carefully designed ‘user journey’ that we have been using and refining for years. Its aim is to ensure that the vast amount of new information, know-how, terminology, company culture and so on does not overwhelm someone like a deluge, but gradually comes together into a coherent whole: from the first coffee to the first project retrospective.

On their very first day, new starters receive their computer, phone and Works. welcome pack — including a notebook, hoodie and a pack of French playing cards; elderflower cordial has even featured before. We guarantee that you will not have to wait days for an email address or access to SharePoint or Figma here. Everything is available from day one, so new arrivals can immediately feel useful and like a fully-fledged member of the team.

Tamás and/or Ákos from the company leadership personally talk through who we are, the projects we work on and why we operate the way we do. We show them around the office (definitely the coffee machine and the chocolate drawer; the location of the fire extinguisher and the escape route are just the icing on the cake), followed by other everyday but important information: the rules for using the shared kitchen, additional days off on working Saturdays, and at the end of the year, between Christmas and New Year.

### Integration: mentoring, the deep end and lunch

New colleagues soon get to know their mentor, with whom they discuss the events of the previous week in regular 1:1s. Mentoring is partly structured, but it can be longer or shorter, more or less frequent, depending on the new team member’s needs. This arrangement continues throughout the probation period, then evolves as needed in line with the professional and organisational challenges ahead.

At the end of the probation period, Tamás and Ákos, the company leaders, hold a review meeting with the new colleague. Together, they look back on the experiences of the initial period and identify further areas for professional and personal development.

Meanwhile, we naturally begin to explore how we work. At Works., this means both professional development and calibrating one’s perspective. For junior colleagues, the first few months are about learning the fundamentals of research and design methodologies, project management and client work. For more experienced colleagues, it is about understanding the ‘Works.’ methodology and how we think as a team.

The ‘deep end’ is real here: everyone joins a project relatively quickly. But that does not mean we leave people to fend for themselves. No one works alone; there is always someone to discuss emerging questions and dilemmas with — whether that is their mentor, the project lead or simply a more experienced colleague.

It is very rare for someone to be assigned outsourced work in their first few weeks. We find it useful and necessary for everyone to go through a kind of ‘incubation’ period: first getting to know the team’s rhythm, our internal ways of working and our shared language. Once the right level of confidence has been built, it is easier to demonstrate what they can do on the client side.

From Monday to Friday, when midday comes around, there is no question: we have lunch together. It is one of Works.’ most enduring traditions. Some new arrivals are surprised by it, but they usually get the hang of it quickly. Around the table, we talk about projects, trashy reality TV, football, hiking, theatre — in short, anything.

### A learning organisation

An organisational development partner once said that we are a *learning organisation*. We think so too. But for us, learning is primarily not about training courses; it is about continuous experimentation and *daring*to ask new questions — which is when we realise just how much we do not yet know that we do not know.

Questioning, learning and experimentation happen in our internal professional forums: specialist groups and village meetings (aka all-hands meetings). Everyone takes part: there are exciting project reports, inspiring professional workshops, quarterly financial summaries and strategic outlooks for the future. Sharing experiences, dilemmas, and good and bad moments is what makes us a team.

### What really matters

Our everyday work combines structure and flexibility. We know that in a small Hungarian company, attention is the scarcest resource. It is difficult to make time for a new arrival, which is precisely why we consciously structure the first few months. Mentoring, daily shared lunches and internal forums all serve the same purpose: ensuring that new starters do not just get here, but truly arrive with us.

At Works., we do not expect someone to know everything in their first week. Instead, we want them to feel able to ask questions, make mistakes, connect with others and gradually become part of the team. We also provide a framework for development: our grade system helps everyone see where they are heading, the direction in which they need and want to develop, and what support they need to do so. Over the years, this system has also been refined through several iterations, and is now a natural part of our feedback culture. We do not consider it a success simply that our colleagues work at Works.; it is when they consider themselves ‘Works. people’.
This article was written by Horváth László, Senior Experience Designer at Works.

blogPosts.title: Why do CX initiatives fail, and how can AI help?
blogPosts.excerpt: CX initiatives often stall not because of a lack of intent, but because learning is slow, data is fragmented and insights are not incorporated into decisions. AI can help at these points: it uncovers connections faster, creates a shared interpretive framework, and brings customer insights and development decisions closer together.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Miért buknak el a CX-kezdeményezések és hogyan segíthet ebben az AI?

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_miert_buknak_el_a_cx_kezdemenyezesek_1_d2c3eb4fd4.png

### The past 10 years of customer experience management

Customer centricity is no longer simply a positive attitude; it is an operating model. Organisations treat customer experience (CX) as a core value, learn from their customers on an ongoing basis, and incorporate that learning into their decision-making processes. Over the past decade, this approach has delivered more stable growth in many places, as retention has finally come into focus alongside customer acquisition. Research, feedback and testing have replaced ‘we think this is right’. Omnichannel thinking has gained ground, reducing friction between channels and creating a more consistent experience. Programmes designed to improve customer experience have also raised baseline quality expectations, so in many industries today, a good experience is not an extra but the minimum requirement. It has had a cultural impact, too: empathy and the processing of customer feedback have become part of organisations’ everyday practice.

At the same time, CX has often stalled not because there was no intent, but because organisations did not make the shift at a systemic level. The most common issue was **a lack of ownership**: if no one is accountable for the experience at journey level, it becomes everyone’s responsibility and no one’s. In many places, measurement and reporting were implemented, but **the insight–backlog–development process was not established**. The operating rhythm was typically reactive: we learned in **monthly or quarterly** cycles, while **experience problems emerged more quickly than that**. Finally, short-term business pressure often overrode experience improvements that would have paid off over the longer term. **The lesson of the decade** is therefore that CX only creates lasting value when it is not a series of projects, but **an integrated system that learns quickly and is founded on sound decisions**. Seen this way, the CX story of the past decade is both a success story and an unfinished sentence: we have learned to do many things well, but repeatedly got stuck at critical points in the system.

With the arrival of artificial intelligence, we now have a technological toolkit that can make a meaningful difference precisely in these areas.

### AI opportunities in customer experience

### 1) Efficiency

AI can make an impact on CX where these systems have repeatedly fallen short: **speed, uncovering connections and efficiently supporting decision-making**. Over the past decade, many organisations have learned to measure customer experience, but AI now gives us the opportunity **not to stop at recording what happens**,**but** **to quickly identify the patterns and causes behind it**. In other words, we can see not only where the experience is deteriorating, but also what is driving it down and where it is worth intervening before problems become visible in KPIs. What used to involve weekly or monthly analysis cycles, manual categorisation and retrospective reporting can now **move closer to real time**. Not because we will have more data, but because **AI can continuously process signals arriving from different channels**, identify patterns and breaks in trends, and **provide early warnings** before KPIs deteriorate noticeably.

### 2) A shared interpretive framework

The second major transformation takes place **at the level of meaning**. Information coming from CX is inherently heterogeneous: written complaints, tickets, survey scores, usage logs and qualitative interviews have often spoken different languages. AI delivers a step change when it creates **a shared interpretive framework from this diversity**: drawing on a unified taxonomy, it can **gather evidence from multiple sources** for the same issue and map **cause-and-effect relationships** more quickly. This also **transforms the role of KPIs**: they are no longer the endpoint, but **‘merely’ symptoms**, potentially underpinned by causes at journey level. The emphasis subtly shifts **from seeking correlations towards explanatory logic**, bringing a new level of quality to CX analysis, even at an expert level.

### 3) Decision integration

The third, and perhaps most important, change is **decision integration**. AI does not make decisions for organisations, but it redraws the path from insight to intervention: it **offers prioritisation recommendations**, runs ‘what if’ scenarios, and **helps estimate business impact**. This is critical because CX’s weakness to date has been that momentum disappeared between analysis and development decisions. If learning and decision-making move closer together, CX **will no longer be about producing reports, but will become part of the development logic**. In short, AI does not change the purpose of CX; it makes how it operates faster, more sensitive to connections and better equipped for decision-making.

### Where should you start?

### 1) Think small

If an organisation wants to integrate AI into its CX operations now, the biggest mistake is trying to build a ‘large system’ straight away. A better starting point is to select one or two areas where slowness or fragmentation already causes pain, and begin experimenting there with AI support on a small scale. Establishing a POC-based approach offers a good opportunity for this (POC = proof of concept). Typical examples include **speeding up insight processing** (such as consistently tagging and making complaints, tickets and research materials searchable), or introducing **an early warning system (warnings)** for critical journeys.

### 2) Creating a shared language

Another important first step is **creating a shared language**. AI can be used effectively in CX when it is clear which customer experience dimensions we are monitoring, how we name the same problem across different channels, and who is responsible for turning learning into change. This is not a technology issue, but an operating model: taxonomy, ownership and decision-making rhythm. With this framework in place, AI does not simply sit on top of existing chaos; it begins to bring order to it. From there, it becomes much easier to expand the system step by step: with more and more data sources, increasingly precise cause-and-effect logic, and ever stronger decision support.
The author is **Ákos Maczinkó**, Managing Director of Works.

blogPosts.title: Which digital accessibility service do you need? We’ll help you choose!
blogPosts.excerpt: There is no single right approach to digital accessibility for every situation. From risk assessments and detailed audits to training and user testing with people with disabilities, different approaches can help depending on where an organisation is in its journey. This article will help you choose which service is the best fit and when.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Milyen digitális akadálymentesítési szolgáltatásra van szükséged? Segítünk választani!

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_milyen_digitalis_akadalymentesitesi_szolgaltatasra_van_szukseged_1_72344805d9.jpg
content.caption: Accessibility is not a luxury but a basic principle – just like fresh bread.
content.alt: A hozzáférhetőség nem luxus, hanem alapvetés: akárcsak a friss kenyér.

content.content:
Much has already been written – including by Works. colleagues – about what digital accessibility means in practice, who the law applies to, and what to consider during design and development to ensure a digital interface meets the requirements.

In this article, we introduce our services and help you decide which one to choose and when.

### 1. Risk assessment – the ‘small audit’

If you need an initial assessment of your current situation, we recommend a risk assessment. This review covers a smaller, predefined set of pages, and the audit is carried out on just one device and operating system. It focuses primarily on the most critical errors that hinder use, as well as those most commonly found on the websites of organisations in the relevant industry.

### When should you choose it?

We recommend it to clients who are just starting to address accessibility but are unsure where to begin. It can also be useful for teams whose development capacity is fully allocated, or who simply need a quick, affordable way to identify pain points and the most commonly occurring errors.

### What will you get from us?

The approach is based on exploratory assessment and the Pareto principle: we identify the error types that occur most often, as well as issues that cause users to get stuck. The findings document presents WCAG violations through specific examples and suggests the expertise required to fix them.

### Limitations

Risk assessment has limitations that are worth considering before you choose it:

- As this is not an audit but a risk assessment, the service is not intended to uncover every error that may occur. This means some errors may remain undiscovered and unresolved.

- Not every commonly occurring, typical error is listed; instead, we use examples and descriptions to support the discovery of other errors.

### 2. Detailed accessibility audit

During a detailed audit, we use a methodology developed by our team to uncover errors across the interface. This ensures that, beyond clearly obstructive issues, we also identify problems that violate less obvious and more difficult-to-grasp WCAG success criteria.

### When should you choose it?

We recommend this service to clients who have already completed accessibility improvements and would like to carry out a ‘re-audit’ to address any remaining errors. It can also be useful for teams able to fix the issues identified shortly after the audit, so that no major changes are made to the site between the audit and the fixes. It can also help clarify exactly which requirements the interface needs to meet, supporting the prevention of future errors.

### What will you get from us?

A comprehensive audit covering every issue across desktop and mobile environments. The findings document includes a detailed list of errors, WCAG references, recommended fixes and the role most likely responsible.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_milyen_digitalis_akadalymentesitesi_szolgaltatasra_van_szukseged_2_d96a189485.jpg
content.caption: Screen Reader, Accessibility Testing, Alt Text. Illustrations from the Accessibility Icon Collection.
content.alt: Screen Reader, Accessibility Testing, Alt Text. Illusztrációk az Accessibility Icon Collection ből.

content.content:
### 3. Accessibility training

The aim of our two-day, practice-focused training is to build accessibility awareness and knowledge within your organisation. Participants learn the theoretical foundations (the legal background, types of disability and statistics), WCAG standards, and how to independently check accessibility using manual and automated tools. They also receive support in correctly interpreting the results of audits carried out by us, ensuring that they can provide feedback to developers or designers without our help in the future.

### When should you choose it?

We recommend this service to clients who have already completed at least one expert audit and fixed the issues identified, while continuing to update their interfaces. This means they do not need to turn to an external auditor before every update. It can also be useful for teams looking to build in-house capability and reduce costs in the long term.

### What will you get from us?

A two-day, practice-focused training course covering the legal background, types of disability and WCAG criteria, as well as the fundamentals of auditing on your team’s own website. By the end of the training, the team will have jointly created its own error-list template, which we will also apply in practice during the exercises.

### 4. User testing with people with disabilities – real experiences, real feedback

Some of the most valuable feedback comes directly from the people affected. In our user tests, we involve testers with disabilities who, beyond sharing their general experiences, can provide feedback on a live interface. We recruit testers from our own reliable database, which includes participants with a range of disabilities in addition to visually impaired users.

### When should you choose it?

We primarily recommend it to teams that have already fixed the issues found in audits, and perhaps also completed a re-audit, but want to carry out one final check of the interface to filter out blocking and more serious problems. We can also use this type of test in specialist environments that cannot be effectively assessed using conventional audit methodology, such as TVs, kiosks, POS systems and other hardware interfaces.

### What will you get from us?

- **UX interviews**Structured conversations in which users share their experiences, difficulties and observations while using the digital interface.

- **Bug-finding test**A specialised form of functional testing, supplemented with accessibility considerations. The aim is for participants to find as many issues as possible, including errors that cause users to get stuck. We then categorise and assess these using the WCAG-based framework we have developed. While this method does not replace an accessibility audit, it is excellent for identifying the most serious issues.

### Further reading

If you would like to read more about accessibility, take a look at our earlier articles on the subject:

- [**8 common issues a digital accessibility audit reveals – and how you could easily avoid them**](https://worksdot.hu/blog/8-gyakori-hiba-amit-egy-digitalis-akadalymentessegi-audit-feltar)
- [**Accessibility audit: functional testing or UX research?**](https://worksdot.hu/blog/akadalymentes-audit-funkcionalis-teszt-vagy-ux-kutatas)
- [**Digital accessibility – the basics**](https://worksdot.hu/blog/digitalis-akadalymentesites)

**We work at several levels, using several methods, but with one goal:**to make your digital services accessible to everyone – not only because it is a legal obligation, but because it is the foundation of a more inclusive, open digital world.

If you have any questions about our services, or are unsure which direction is right for your team, please get in touch!
The author is Eszter Kemper-Ángyán, Experience Designer and accessibility expert at Works.

blogPosts.title: Does AI make UX research more accessible — or offer a cheap illusion?
blogPosts.excerpt: AI is revolutionising UX research — but perhaps not in the way we might first expect. While more and more tools promise fast, affordable solutions, genuine understanding remains a human task. The question is not whether AI will replace researchers, but whether it can help us understand people more deeply.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Elérhetőbbé teszi az AI a UX-kutatást – vagy csak olcsó illúziót kínál?

content.content: The rapid development of AI is transforming UX research too. But does it truly democratise research, or simply offer a quick, cheap illusion?
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_elerhetobbe_teszi_az_ai_a_ux_kutatast_vagy_csak_olcso_illuziot_kinal_1_59bc8ed681.png
content.caption: AI democratises research, but it does not replace people. It is a collaboration that can only be productive in human hands. (Image generated by DALL-E)
content.alt: Az AI demokratizálja a kutatást, de nem váltja ki az embert. Ez egy olyan együttműködés, ami csak egy ember keze alatt lehet termékeny. (DALL-E generálta kép)

content.content:
### TL;DR (If you don’t have time to read)

AI democratises UX research, but it does not replace people. The real question is not ‘will AI replace researchers?’, but **how they can work together in a smarter, more effective UX research ecosystem.**

**Why is democratising research a good thing?**

Because it gives not only researchers but other team members access to user insights, supporting more empathetic decision-making.

**What are the risks of AI research?**

AI models often rely on statistical averages, which can skew results, especially for specialist target groups.

**Can AI replace researchers?**

No. AI helps with routine tasks, but human empathy, sensitivity to context and strategic thinking are irreplaceable.

**What are synthetic personas?**

They are AI models trained on a particular target group, providing fast but not necessarily in-depth feedback.

### AI is changing the world of research

The rapid development of AI is transforming UX research too. A growing number of tools can provide basic UX feedback, analyse prototypes or even run synthetic ‘user tests’. This raises an intriguing question: could AI make UX research more widely accessible?

### Why is research becoming more accessible now?

Previously, UX research and usability testing were too expensive or time-consuming for many businesses. AI, however, can provide basic feedback on a new website, form or app quickly and affordably. This means that teams that previously had no opportunity to conduct UX research can now receive guidance.
*‘Just as Figma democratised design… AI tools are democratising research.’ (Shrey Khokhra, Userology)*

### What are the risks of AI research?

Skipping UX research and replacing it entirely with AI presents both an opportunity and a risk.

AI-generated feedback is often generic: it is based on statistical averages and does not reflect real people’s real feelings. AI models are not yet able to represent more specific target groups well — for example, users defined by their profession, life circumstances or culture — because they have not been trained to do so.

What AI provides is fast but only approximate feedback, rather than deep understanding. It is therefore worth considering the scale of the decision being based on this data, and the business risk that follows. 
The greater the impact of a decision, the stronger the case for research with real users.

### Middle-ground solutions: synthetic personas
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_elerhetobbe_teszi_az_ai_a_ux_kutatast_vagy_csak_olcso_illuziot_kinal_2_93f7f2d651.jpg
content.caption: Illustration of a synthetic persona
content.alt: Illusztráció a szintetikus perszónáról

content.content:
There are middle-ground solutions, too: for example, creating data-driven synthetic personas — AI models trained specifically for a particular target group. They can provide feedback more frequently and quickly, but creating them requires effort, so they are worthwhile when used regularly.

With synthetic personas, there is a further risk: their ‘knowledge’ is based partly on the language model’s general training data and partly on a targeted, specialist dataset. It is difficult to determine how much a particular response draws on one or the other — which may affect the accuracy of the results.

### ‘Democratising’ research within the organisation

UX research is becoming more accessible not only because more companies can use it, but also because other departments within larger organisations — product teams, marketers and customer service teams — can more easily conduct research themselves and access research findings.
*‘Democratising research means enabling anyone across the organisation to responsibly conduct research, consume user insights and act on them.’ (UX Army blog, 2024)*
As a result, understanding of and empathy for customers can develop more easily within the organisation.
*‘The closer people are to the user, the stronger their empathy towards them.’ (LogRocket blog, 2023)*

### The role of researchers is not disappearing — it is changing

The role of UX researchers is not disappearing — it is changing. The real value of the work lies not in producing questionnaires or test scripts, but in thinking, recognising patterns and interpreting human behaviour.

Artificial intelligence helps with routine tasks, but empathy, strategic thinking and understanding context remain human responsibilities. Researchers have an increasingly important role in ensuring that generated insights are genuinely embedded in decisions. As research findings become accessible to everyone — or at least many people — within an organisation, researchers must also support the organisation in processing, interpreting and incorporating them into day-to-day work.

The researcher’s role therefore grows in helping to establish and strengthen a customer-centric culture within the company. In this way, AI opens up new opportunities.

### Sources

- [Brilliantexperience.com](https://www.brilliantexperience.com/blog/democratizing-ux-research-using-ai-interview-with-shrey-khokhra-userology?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
- [uxarmy.com](https://uxarmy.com/blog/democratise-with-ux-research-platforms/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
- [logrocket.com](https://blog.logrocket.com/product-management/what-is-user-research-democratization-why-does-it-matter/)
The author is Tamás Lichter, Managing Director of Works.

blogPosts.title: How does it all come together?
blogPosts.excerpt: A year and a half ago, we were still conducting research manually and intuitively. Today, we have a new companion at our side: AI. What value does it add when involved from the very beginning? Using a telecommunications project as an example, we explored the answer – from the brief and hypotheses to the methodology.

content.content:
### How can AI support research preparation? Rethinking a real project

The following article is based on the presentation of the same title by [Balázs Dombóvári and László Horváth](/en/about), prepared for this year's Service Design Day conference (SDD 2025).

At SDD, the Works. team devoted an entire morning to presenting the opportunities we see in AI in autumn 2025, and where we currently stand in optimising our own research processes with its help.

Balázs and Laci examined the beginning of the research process, with particular attention to interpreting the brief and selecting the right methodology.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_mi_a_kutatas_elokesziteseben_1_9faed93262.png
content.caption: Auguste Rodin's and DALL-E's sculptures titled “The Thinker”, facing one another
content.alt: Auguste Rodin és a DALL-E “A gondolkodó” c. szobrai egymással szemben

content.content:
### An enquiry from spring 2024

Last spring, we received a brief from one of our telecommunications partners that was roughly as follows:

*"Several user issues and criticisms have arisen regarding the TV remote controls currently in use. Help us develop the ideal TV remote-control concept: a simpler, more intuitive solution tailored to user needs."*

At the time, following the traditional approach, we:

- interpreted the **brief**,
- formulated **hypotheses** and then **research questions**,
- selected the **methodology**,
- then developed the tools used for the study (**discussion guide, questionnaire, interview guide**).

It was a creative process on a human scale. We were also familiar with **researcher loneliness**: that state when you are scrolling through a list of hypotheses on screen, wondering whether these really are the most appropriate questions.

### What if we were starting today?

What would we do differently if we were embarking on the same project today? How would **artificial intelligence** support our work? This thought experiment was not about automating research and removing people from the process entirely. Rather, it was about exploring how AI could become an **assistant** and thinking partner, and how it might affect the **researcher’s role**.

### 1. Brief

The very first phase of research is interpretation. A brief always originates from the client's perspective, and our task is to uncover its **underlying layers**, **real expectations** and **assumptions**. Of course, an experienced researcher can draw these out of the business in a workshop – they simply need to keep asking: “Why?”

While asking follow-up questions remains important, using **AI** as a **question generator** could shorten the time between receiving the brief and preparing a proposal. How?

*“We are a consultancy specialising in Service Design / UX Design / UX Research, and we have received the following brief from a Hungarian telecommunications company: [brief goes here] Help us with questions: which areas require further clarification before we can prepare a professional proposal in response to this brief?”*

The response gave us what we expected: **new perspectives** – similar to ones we had prepared for ourselves, but not all of them and not quite in this form.

A few examples of the questions:

- Is the remote-control development a standalone project, or part of a broader **product or service development** initiative?
- What is the client's **definition of success**: cost reduction, user satisfaction, fewer customer service calls…?
- In what situations is the remote control used: traditional TV viewing, streaming, gaming, smart home control?
- Which devices does the remote control need to operate?
- Are there any **brand strategy or technological constraints**?
- Who makes the decision, and how many levels of approval are required?
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_mi_a_kutatas_elokesziteseben_2_0fefecf951.png
content.caption: This is often what AI-generated answers are like: of course we knew it – we just had not thought of it.
content.alt: Sokszor ilyenek az MI által generált válaszok: Persze, hogy tudtuk, csak nem sejtettük.

content.content:
### 2. Hypotheses

Next, we explored what hypotheses AI would form based on our partner’s personas.

What both approaches had in common:

- they assumed different **usage patterns** (background viewing, intentional content consumption, etc.),
- they assumed different **levels of user knowledge**,
- and they recognised that the **role of streaming** has become more important compared with linear TV viewing.

### The expert thought at a systems level

- examining the **service experience** and the **entire ecosystem**,
- taking **temporal and social patterns** into account,
- identifying specific **usability challenges**,
- and considering how a device could replace other functions within the household.

### AI’s focus was operational and role-based

- it wrote **hypotheses assigned to personas**, and
- focused on the remote control’s specific features and modes of use.

So **AI** did not think for us; instead, it **opened up a new perspective** on the same problem. While we were thinking at a systems level, it was looking for patterns at a micro level.

### A prompt is like research

For both, **the quality of the input determines the output**. The more precise the prompt (or research question), the more reliable the response (and the research findings).

### 3. Methodology

We originally used a mixed-methods approach for the project:

1. **Think-aloud videos** with users, based on a defined scenario
2. **Co-creation workshop with users** to prototype the remote control
3. **Co-creation workshop with the expert team** to narrow down and select potential directions

AI also introduced alternative methodologies, including:

1. **Interviews in the home environment** 
We had considered this, but ruled it out for cost-efficiency reasons.
2. **Clickable prototype** 
We had considered this, but felt that, as it is a physical object, it would be difficult to assess virtually, potentially skewing the results significantly. If complemented by testing a physical prototype, however, it could be worth considering.
3. **Online questionnaire validation of the prototype** 
This had not occurred to us, and we still do not consider it a good idea today; see the previous point.
4. **Expert remote-control analysis workshop** 
This had not occurred to us at all: our client specifically wanted to amplify the voice of customers, rather than hear expert opinions.

### Final thoughts

Using artificial intelligence can be a huge help even in the early stages of research:

1. **It broadens perspectives effectively**: it brings new considerations and alternative approaches, while enabling dialogue and rapid iteration.
2. **It eliminates researcher isolation** – a companion when working through dilemmas, if there is nobody to bounce ideas off.
3. **For less experienced researchers**, it can provide – sometimes perhaps misleadingly – **confidence**, helping them structure their questions and recognise missing connections.
4. It can formulate **questions tailored to the industry and business context**.
5. Does it make work faster? Yes. But more importantly, it can **improve quality**.
6. The key principle of working with AI is this: **weak input leads to weak output**. AI **does not automate; it assists** – supporting, helping to structure and inspiring.
7. **Responsibility still lies with people**. For now, **the researcher is still the one who makes the decision at the end of the day**.
This article was written by Horváth László, Senior Experience Designer at Works.

blogPosts.title: 8 common issues a digital accessibility audit reveals – and you could easily avoid
blogPosts.excerpt: During an accessibility audit, small technical or design issues often create the biggest barriers to use. This article presents eight typical problems that can be avoided during design and development with the right approach and a few considered decisions.
blogPosts.imageAlt: 8 gyakori hiba, amit egy digitális akadálymentességi audit feltár – és amit könnyen elkerülhetnél

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_8_gyakori_hiba_amit_egy_digitalis_akadalymentessegi_audit_feltar_1_d34c61ab76.png
content.caption: Three icons from the Accessibility Icon Collection
content.alt: Három ikon az Accessibility Icon Collection ből

content.content:
Many people assume that if a website “works” and looks visually polished, it is equally accessible to all users. In reality, most sites are full of barriers that are invisible at first glance – unless you try using them with a screen reader, keyboard or other assistive technology.

The purpose of a digital accessibility audit is precisely to uncover these “invisible issues”. Below, we have collected eight common problems that come up time and again during audits – and that are relatively easy to fix.

### 1. Inadequate contrast ratio – “ahem, as is well known”

“Is it well known? I’m afraid, Safranek, that you are making fun of me. Come closer!” This excerpt comes from the evergreen animated film Catcatcher, although it was not quite about accessibility’s best-known requirement.

Dove-grey text on an ash-grey background? It can look beautiful, but it is not easy for everyone to read. For visually impaired or older users, as well as people browsing on their phones outdoors, it can be a significant barrier.

The WCAG recommendation: a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_8_gyakori_hiba_amit_egy_digitalis_akadalymentessegi_audit_feltar_2_8eeb4adef2.png
content.caption: Figure 1: Good and bad examples of background-to-text contrast ratios.
content.alt: 1. ábra: Jó és rossz példák háttér és szöveg kontrasztarányára.

content.content:
### 2. Missing or incorrect alternative text (alt text)

Screen readers do not “see” images – only their alt text. If this is missing or uninformative (a classic example of uninformative alt text is “image1.jpg”), visual content is lost to people using screen readers.

Every meaningful image should have concise, informative alt text!
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_8_gyakori_hiba_amit_egy_digitalis_akadalymentessegi_audit_feltar_3_318f45da93.png
content.caption: Figure 2: Without alternative text: there is no alt= attribute, so the screen reader cannot provide visually impaired users with information about the programme.
content.alt: 2. ábra: Helyettesítő szöveg nélkül: nincs alt= kiegészítés, így a felolvasó nem tud támpontot adni a programról a látássérülteknek.

content.content:
### 3. Missing heading structure or incorrect heading order

Headings are important not only visually, but structurally too. A well-formed H1–H2–H3 hierarchy helps screen-reader users jump between sections of content – much as we scan a page with our eyes.

A common mistake is omitting the H1 or displaying headings in an inconsistent order.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_8_gyakori_hiba_amit_egy_digitalis_akadalymentessegi_audit_feltar_4_385581e9df.png
content.caption: Figure 3: Incorrectly used heading structure – text displayed as a subheading is not marked as such in the code
content.alt: 3. ábra: Nem jól használt címsorstuktúra – alcímként megjelenő szöveg kódban nem jelölve

content.content:
### 4. The site cannot be used with a keyboard alone

If it is not possible to navigate through a site using the Tab key, users with motor impairments are effectively excluded. This can be particularly problematic in forms, menus and modal windows.

Tip: try navigating the entire site using only Tab and Enter!

### 5. No visual focus indicator

When an interactive element (such as a button or link) receives keyboard focus, this should also be indicated visually. If it is not visible, users do not know where they are – this is not only an accessibility issue, but also a usability problem.

In the example below, the Services item in the menu does not receive an outline when focused, while the Sales menu item does receive a visual indicator.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_8_gyakori_hiba_amit_egy_digitalis_akadalymentessegi_audit_feltar_5_9442794b13.png
content.caption: Figure 4: Good and bad examples of focus indicators
content.alt: 4. ábra: Jó és rossz példa fókuszjelzésre

content.content:
### 6. Buttons and links are not understandable without context

“Details” or “Continue” – but details of what? A user browsing with a screen reader hears only the link, not the context around it.

Solution: use more informative links, such as “Details about our services”.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_8_gyakori_hiba_amit_egy_digitalis_akadalymentessegi_audit_feltar_6_7b63cc1cdc.png
content.caption: Figure 5: Button text without context
content.alt: 5. ábra: Kontextus nélküli gomb szöveg

content.content:
### 7. Missing labels for form fields

Form fields often have no proper labels, only placeholder text – which screen readers frequently cannot interpret. This is one of the most common barriers to completing forms.

Tip: always use a properly associated <label> element for every field.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_8_gyakori_hiba_amit_egy_digitalis_akadalymentessegi_audit_feltar_7_110bdf47e9.png
content.caption: Figure 6: Missing label field on the login form
content.alt: 6. ábra: hiányzó label mező a bejelentkezésnél

content.content:
### 8. Error messages communicated by colour alone

For example, if you mark an invalid form field only in red, people with colour vision deficiency or users of screen readers will not notice the issue.

Combine colour with a written error message or icons!
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_8_gyakori_hiba_amit_egy_digitalis_akadalymentessegi_audit_feltar_8_0f287566e3.png
content.caption: Figure 7: Missing information in the first-name field indicated by colour alone
content.alt: 7. ábra: Csak színnel jelölt hiányzó adat a keresztnév mezőben

content.content:
### Summary

These issues are not technically complex, yet they can easily exclude some users. An accessibility audit is not only about complying with legislation: it also supports a better user experience, reaching a wider audience and building your brand.

If you would like to know how accessible your own website is, get in touch about a digital accessibility audit – we can help you find (and fix) hidden barriers.

**Read more articles on this topic:**

[Accessibility audit: functional testing or UX research?](https://worksdot.hu/blog/akadalymentes-audit-funkcionalis-teszt-vagy-ux-kutatas)

[Digital accessibility – the basics](https://worksdot.hu/blog/digitalis-akadalymentesites)

[Accessibility is a right, not a good deed](https://worksdot.hu/blog/akadalymentesseg-jog-nem-jo-cselekedet)

blogPosts.title: Why do company values matter?
blogPosts.excerpt: For years, we have been looking for ways to work well as a team. The values we have defined together help us understand one another better and move forward more consciously.

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_miert_fontosak_a_ceges_ertekek_1_c644945eca.jpeg
content.caption: Team-building painting session in December 2023
content.alt: Csapatépítő közös festés 2023 decemberében

content.content:
As a company leader, I regularly ask myself how mature our company is. Alongside financial indicators, it is equally important to me how much we have developed in terms of team cohesion. Over the past nearly 10 years, we have never had more than 25 people at one time, yet more than 50 colleagues have worked with us in total during this period. But how can organisational maturity be measured? What can we use as a benchmark to determine our level of development in a constantly changing environment? I believe that the presence of clearly defined company values, and their role within the organisation, can help us assess this.

In a creative business, company values are not merely good-sounding words on a website or in a brand strategy – they are the foundation of everyday decisions and teamwork. Working according to clearly defined values helps hold the team together, makes decision-making faster and more effective, and ensures that the business remains true to its principles in the long term. It also allows us to keep reviewing whether our team dynamics and collaboration are developing in the right direction.

For example, if a junior designer disagrees with decisions made during UI design but does not dare to say that the planned website visuals are not working particularly well, because they feel that, as someone less experienced, they should not criticise them, this will hold the team back in the long term. However, if honest feedback is one of the company’s core values and we actively practise it – for example, by holding a ‘feedback round’ at the end of every meeting – everyone will understand that constructive feedback is not criticism for its own sake, but an opportunity to improve.

An important milestone in the life of our team came at the beginning of 2024, when we finally defined Works.’ values with the involvement of the entire team. Here are some experiences and lessons from the past year:

- **Once shared values have been established, they should always remain visible.** Everyone should encounter them in everyday life. For us, the subject was relatively quickly forgotten last year and did not consciously form part of our daily work. **Now, however, as we are decorating the office, we will put our values up on the walls.**To prepare for this, at our most recent team discussion we collected stories that clearly demonstrate the presence or absence of each value. I felt that this helped colleagues internalise them. We also articulated our beliefs in complete sentences. Here they are:
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_miert_fontosak_a_ceges_ertekek_2_8259841311.png
content.caption: Community lies at the heart of Works.’ philosophy. We believe in the creative power of human collaboration and in making the world more liveable through our work, step by step. Empathy, mutual trust and respect guide our perspective...
content.alt: A Works. filozófiájának középpontjában a közösség áll. Hiszünk az emberi együttműködés teremtő erejében. Hiszünk abban, hogy munkánkkal a világot lépésről-lépésre élhetőbb hellyé varázsoljuk. Látásmódunkat az empátia, a kölcsönös bizalom és tisztelet határozza meg. Így partneri viszonyt alakítunk ki szakértőink és ügyfeleink között, amire igazán büszkék vagyunk. Évtizedes tapasztalatunk bizonyítja hitelességünket, visszatérő ügyfélkörünk pedig a megbízhatóságunkat. Életigenlő, a világra nyitott csapatként működünk, akik folyamatosan alkalmazkodnak a változó piaci igényekhez. Izgatottan követjük a szakma újdonságait és elébe megyünk a trendeknek. Rugalmasan, agilis módon közelítjük meg a feladatokat, és elkötelezettek vagyunk az elérhető legjobb megoldás kidolgozása mellett.

content.content:
- **Values should not be abstract; they should be concrete guidelines that inspire action and can be translated into how we operate**. It is not enough to create words; they must also be given substance. For some time now, we have held a full-day monthly ‘town hall’ (= professional development day). We talk a lot, discuss our field and also focus on the team’s mental wellbeing. Often indirectly, we examine how we work internally through the lens of our values.

- **Sharing lived experiences helps people internalise values and connect with them**. We had long tried to hold retrospectives after projects, but this happened in a fairly ad hoc way. Then, last year, we made them mandatory, and now everyone involved discusses each task after it has been completed. Processing lessons learnt, honestly confronting what happened, and voicing both positive and negative experiences all contribute to individual and team development. These retrospective conversations can of course be demanding at times, but they regularly produce clear, practical suggestions that we can incorporate into how we work to improve our efficiency or the quality of our work.

- **Values also need to be communicated externally**. The image people form of our company is significantly shaped by knowing what they can expect from us – and this can even make us accountable for it. We decided to include an introduction to our values in our renewed sales materials, address the topic in job advertisements, and, after all, this post was written for that reason too. 😊

I believe that if our company values truly become part of everyday life and we operate with them consciously in mind, this will not only strengthen team spirit, but also contribute to Works.’ long-term success.

*Ákos*

blogPosts.title: Accessibility audit: functional testing or UX research?
blogPosts.excerpt: Accessibility audits combine characteristics of functional testing and UX research. They resemble both, yet are very different. In this article, Tamás clears things up.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Akadálymentes audit: funkcionális teszt vagy UX kutatás?

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_akadalymentes_audit_funkcionalis_teszt_vagy_ux_kutatas_1_5f0cfd2e1a.png

When discussing accessibility audits with our clients or within the team, we inevitably compare them with our long-established [services](https://worksdot.hu/). Not without reason: an accessibility audit combines characteristics of both functional testing and UX testing. Which service is closer to an accessibility audit: functional testing or UX research? In short: both, and neither. But let’s start at the beginning.

### What is functional testing?

The purpose of functional testing is to compare the implemented system against the plans and identify defects – in other words, points where the system deviates from the specification or from the way the rest of the system works. The outcome of testing is a bug list containing well-documented, reproducible issues. The list generally records objectively existing defects that need fixing – although there are, of course, cases where it is debatable whether a given element is a ‘bug’ or a ‘feature’.

### What is an accessibility audit?

The purpose of an [accessibility audit](https://akadalymentes.worksdot.hu/) is to identify accessibility issues in a digital interface and ensure that all users – including people with disabilities – can use it without barriers. The audit checks compliance with the requirements of the WCAG standard. Its outcome is also a bug list, which likewise contains – for the most part – objective issues.

### Functional testing vs accessibility audits

### Similarities

- Approach – Both processes assess how a system works against **predefined requirements**.
- Objective, measurable results – Both accessibility audits and functional testing focus on objectively existing **issues** that can be reproduced and fixed.
- Documenting errors and issues – Both result in a **bug list**, and resolving it brings the system closer to the expected behaviour.

### Differences

- Focus – Functional testing focuses on how the system **works**, whereas an accessibility audit examines whether the system is **accessible** to all users, including those using assistive technologies.
- Specificity of requirements – The requirements defined in the accessibility standard, [WCAG](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), are phrased fairly broadly. In contrast, functional-testing test cases are based strictly on the specification of the software in question.
- Source of requirements – The requirements used in accessibility audits were developed by the [World Wide Web Consortium (W3C)](http://www.w3c.hu/). They are internationally accepted, have effectively become a standard, and every accessibility audit assesses compliance with these same requirements. Functional testing, on the other hand, uses bespoke test scenarios for the specific system: a test scenario used for one system cannot be applied to another, as they differ from system to system.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_akadalymentes_audit_funkcionalis_teszt_vagy_ux_kutatas_2_7e016c648c.png
content.caption: Key similarities and differences between functional testing and accessibility audits
content.alt: A funkcionális teszt és az akadálymentes audit főbb hasonlóságai és különbségei

content.content:
### UX testing vs accessibility audits

The purpose of UX testing – also known as usability testing or UX research – is to understand users’ needs, behaviours and problems, so that a more intuitive, efficient and enjoyable digital experience can be created on that basis. It examines how users interact with a product or service, where they get stuck, and what would help them use and enjoy a particular digital interface smoothly.

Now let’s compare UX research and accessibility audits.

### Similarities

- Goal – Both examine how **usable** a system is for a particular target group and aim to make it more usable.
- Outcome – In both cases, testing results in a **bug list**, although their formats differ (see the differences).
- Recommendations for a better experience – Both methodologies aim not only to identify problems, but also to provide **recommendations** for resolving them.

### Differences

- Specificity of requirements – WCAG requirements are phrased relatively broadly, at least compared with the test scenarios used in functional testing. However, the requirements considered in UX research are **even less specific**. For example, concepts such as understandability and learnability leave considerable room for interpretation.
- Objectivity – Although both result in a bug list, issues identified through UX research are **less objective**. UX researchers often conclude that ‘most users’ understood something in one way or another. By contrast, accessibility audits are more objective: the issues they identify are less a matter of opinion – though accessibility audits also have subjective elements.
- Target group – UX research always examines the behaviour of a defined target group or groups; in other words, a central question in UX research is who the participants are. By contrast, an accessibility audit is **not target-group-specific**: it assesses the interface against a universal set of usability criteria.
- Methodology – UX research always involves test participants, whereas an audit is carried out by an expert auditor. Accordingly, it would theoretically be possible to conduct UX audits and accessibility research too, but in our experience there is currently less client demand for these.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_akadalymentes_audit_funkcionalis_teszt_vagy_ux_kutatas_3_4971e68bed.png
content.caption: Key similarities and differences between UX research and accessibility audits
content.alt: A UX kutatás és az akadálymentes audit főbb hasonlóságai és különbségei

content.content:
### Summary

Accessibility audits share many similarities with both methodologies presented here. In their focus on users, they are closer to UX research; in their specificity and pursuit of objectivity, they are closer to functional testing. This dual nature makes accessibility audits unique, as they must meet both technical requirements and user-experience considerations. While functional testing focuses on whether a system ‘works’, and UX research on whether people ‘enjoy using it’, an accessibility audit sits between the two by examining whether ‘everyone can use it’.

blogPosts.title: Digital accessibility – the essentials
blogPosts.excerpt: From 28 June 2025, digital accessibility is mandatory in Hungary. This article covers the legislation, EU requirements, WCAG levels and implementation steps.

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_digitalis_akadalymentesites_1_9666a5723c.png
content.caption: Three icons from the Accessibility Icon Collection
content.alt: Három ikon az Accessibility Icon Collection ből

content.content:
In Hungary, the law requiring products and services to be accessible, including digital interfaces in the business sector, will come into force in June 2025. [Act XVII of 2022](https://njt.hu/jogszabaly/2022-17-00-00) sets out the general rules for complying with accessibility requirements. The Act will enter into force on 28 June 2025.

### What requirements are in place?

Accessibility requirements are fairly wide-ranging, and it is easy to get lost in the subject. Below, we list those you need to be aware of when working with digital accessibility:

- In Hungary, the primary legislation is Act XVII of 2022, which enters into force on 28 June 2025. This Act refers to the EU [Web Accessibility Directive (2019/882)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/882/oj?locale=hu), effectively transposing it into Hungarian law and supporting compliance with it. It is therefore worth being familiar with it too.
- EU Directive 2019/882, also known as the European Accessibility Act (EAA), aims to create consistent EU-wide rules for digital devices and interfaces provided by the business sector. This Directive also set the 2025 date uniformly across the EU.
- EU Directive 2019/882 refers to the EU [Web Accessibility Directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/hu/LSU/?uri=CELEX:32016L2102) (WAD, Directive 2016/2102), which came earlier. The WAD requires websites and mobile applications belonging to the public and public-service sectors in the EU to comply with accessibility requirements. It entered into force gradually between 2019 and 2021, and was transposed into Hungarian law by Act LXXV of 2018. In other words, the regulator began with itself – the public sector – in pursuing its aim of making services accessible to people with disabilities.
- The basis for implementing the Web Accessibility Directive is the European standard EN 301 549. This is where WCAG comes into the picture, as EN 301 549 requires compliance with WCAG 2.1 at level AA.
- [WCAG 2.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/) (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is one of the most important international standards for accessible web content, developed by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C).

So, Hungarian Act XVII of 2022 transposes EU Directive 2019/882 into domestic law. That Directive ensures alignment with the EU Web Accessibility Directive (2016/2102), which is implemented through the European standard EN 301 549, requiring WCAG 2.1 level AA compliance.

### Who does the domestic law apply to?

Public-sector institutions were already required to make their digital services accessible, including municipalities, state schools and government bodies.

The law applying to the business sector (Act XVII of 2022) explicitly names certain services:

- retail banking services,
- e-commerce services (including the online sale of both products and services),
- audiovisual media services (typically online video platforms),
- e-books,
- self-service terminals,
- electronic communications services,
- public-transport ticketing solutions

The Act limits the above services to:

- services provided by companies to consumers,
- and excludes services provided by microenterprises from its scope.

As a result, most interactive digital interfaces fall within the scope of the Act.

### What requirements must be met?

The Act states that its aim is to ensure that ‘every person, regardless of disability, has access [to digital devices and interfaces] to the fullest extent possible’. We would highlight the following examples across several areas:

### Accessibility of information

- Information about the use of products and services must be made available through multiple sensory channels, for example both visually and in audio form.
- Navigation elements within a website, such as the menu bar and sidebar, must always appear in the same order and location across different subpages.

### Communication options

- Different modes of communication must be provided, such as visual, acoustic, verbal and tactile elements.
- Speech-based devices must offer alternative communication options.

### Using devices

- Visual content must allow users to zoom without losing information, and be compatible with screen-reader software.
- Other means of distinction must be used alongside colour coding.
- Visual cues must be provided alongside audio signals.
- Audio elements must allow users to adjust volume and playback speed, and audio clarity must be ensured.

### Physical access

- Devices must offer alternatives to actions requiring fine motor skills.
- Alternative identification methods must be available alongside biometric identification.

### Accessibility has several levels

WCAG defines three levels of accessibility conformance. The lowest level is A (pronounced ‘single A’), followed by AA (‘double A’) and AAA (‘triple A’).
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_digitalis_akadalymentesites_2_d08332ed6a.png
content.caption: Practical examples of WCAG accessibility levels
content.alt: Működésbeli példák WCAG akadálymentességi szintekre

content.content:
### 1. Level A – Basic accessibility: minimum requirements

Ensuring basic accessibility so that the website is at least partly usable for people with disabilities.

**Examples:**

- Alternative text (alt text) for images
- Providing at least a text transcript for videos
- Navigation that can also be used with a keyboard

### 2. Level AA – Expected accessibility: a legal requirement in many places

Providing better accessibility for most users. The legislation mentioned above (EU Directives 2016/2102 and 2019/882) requires this level.

**Examples:**

- Appropriate text-to-background contrast ratio (at least 4.5:1)
- A responsive interface that works well on mobile devices
- Providing captions for every video
- Clear presentation of error messages and forms

### 3. Level AAA – Advanced accessibility: the ideal level, but neither mandatory nor easy to achieve

The highest level of accessibility, providing a convenient, easily accessible experience for all users. Achieving it may not always be a realistic goal.

**Examples:**

- Even higher text-to-background contrast (at least 7:1)
- Alternative means of communication (e.g. sign language interpretation for videos)
- Providing interactions without time limits

The three levels build on one another. If legal compliance is the goal, Level AA is clearly what we need to aim for.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_digitalis_akadalymentesites_3_843428ccaf.png
content.caption: The levels defined by WCAG build on one another
content.alt: A WCAG által meghatározott szintek egymásra épülnek

content.content:
### Why does this matter?

There are several good answers:

- it is required by law, which may in itself be reason enough.
- there is an economic benefit to developing digital interfaces for a wider audience – and it is not only those directly affected who will find them easier to use. Level AA compliance improves the overall user experience (UX) too (e.g. responsive design, forms that are easier to complete, sufficient time for transactions, etc.)
- taking accessibility into account improves a site's SEO through better-structured content
- the brand experience suffers if an interface does not even meet basic accessibility requirements

### What should I do?

If you are ready to get started, we recommend the following steps:
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_digitalis_akadalymentesites_4_7cc31cc3ab.png
content.caption: Steps towards accessibility
content.alt: Az akadálymentesítés lépései

content.content:
### 1. Accessibility audit

The first step is to assess how well your digital interfaces currently meet accessibility requirements. At Works., we can [help](https://akadalymentes.worksdot.hu/) with this. We have developed a robust accessibility audit methodology that identifies as many issues as possible while offering good value for money. As a result of the audit, you can expect an issue list that several people will need to work on:

- **Developer**: perhaps most tasks will end up with the developer, who will need to adapt the interface at code level so that screen readers can handle it properly, users can navigate without a mouse, and so on.
- **Designer**: the designer will also have tasks from the issue list, as they need to put the interface's information architecture in order and work with colours too (contrast, communicating meaning through colour, etc.).
- **Colleagues responsible for copy** (marketing, product, copywriter, legal): there will be plenty to do with the copy as well, and the other two colleagues will consult them when a business decision is needed.

### 2. Fixing issues

The issue list produced by the accessibility audit needs to be prioritised, then handed over to developers, designers and others, with fixes scheduled together. Once you get this far, you have already taken steps to make your existing interfaces accessible. Not every issue may be fixed immediately, but you are on the right track and making progress.

### 3. Updating the development process

To ensure that meeting accessibility requirements is not a one-off exercise, and that the accessibility of digital interfaces improves continuously, the process through which interfaces are developed needs to change. Regular monitoring of accessibility requirements should be built into this process, for example through recurring audits. This also assumes that knowledge of accessibility requirements has been developed within the organisation, which means providing training for colleagues. You can think of Works. for this too.

### 4. Improving the design process

Best of all, address compliance for digital interfaces right from the start by incorporating accessibility considerations into the design process – in other words, by applying inclusive design. Inclusive design aims to create products, services and experiences that are usable and accessible to everyone. It does not only develop solutions for people with disabilities, but takes into account anyone who may encounter a barrier – even temporarily.

### Summary

We have aimed to provide an overview of applying accessibility considerations and of what to do if you want to start addressing them, whether driven by internal or external motivation. The best place to begin is with an audit, then progress through updating the development process towards inclusive design.

We would be happy to help with these tasks. Find out more on our [website](https://akadalymentes.worksdot.hu/).

blogPosts.title: Research trends in 2025
blogPosts.excerpt: In recent years, demand for customer research has grown significantly, driven by the combined effect of several factors. Read Ákos’s latest blog post for insights from recent years and the developments ahead.

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_kutatasi_trendek_2025_ben_1_d020ff777b.jpg

### Research has come of age

In recent years, demand for customer research has grown significantly, driven by the combined effect of several factors.

On the one hand, customers have increasingly high expectations of digital products and services — they expect seamless, personalised and intuitive experiences.

On the other, design organisations within large companies are becoming more mature: research processes are being integrated into decision-making, and a deep understanding of user needs is becoming an unbeatable competitive advantage.

Finally, technological advances — such as automated analysis, more advanced data analysis tools and more accessible testing platforms — make research faster, more accurate and potentially more cost-effective. Customer research has now found its rightful place in product and service development: decision-makers now see it as a critical step.

### Combined methodologies

As user research becomes more widespread, organisations are becoming more deliberate in designing and developing user experiences. As a result, they are now also open to using combined research methodologies within individual projects. In one of our projects, for example, we helped define the app development roadmap for a telecommunications provider. We first mapped out typical personas based on different customer behaviours through an online survey, then gained detailed insights into each persona’s attitudes through in-depth interviews. At a later stage, we validated the designed user journeys through further customer interviews.

### Repetition is the mother of risk reduction
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_kutatasi_trendek_2025_ben_2_3548ff3e69.jpg

Research is often no longer conducted only at the initial design stage of products, but repeatedly across different phases of development. This gives teams continuous feedback and enables them to respond more flexibly to changing needs. This approach supports not only a better user experience but also reduces risk, as issues can be identified and corrected earlier. Overall, embedding regular research into processes contributes to creating more market-ready, user-centred products.

Alongside the growing role of user research, several new trends have emerged in this field in recent years:

### Customer experience in BPR

It is increasingly common for customer experience to become a key consideration in BPR (Business Process Reengineering) projects too. In several of our projects, our recommendations for improving internal processes and operations were guided by the impact that changes would have on the customer experience. Our clients are increasingly open to this approach, too. In some cases, clients have rejected a more cost-effective solution if it would have caused customer frustration.

### Specialist target groups

At the same time, research target groups are becoming increasingly specialised — whether narrow professional communities, such as registered solar panel installers; hard-to-reach consumer segments, such as busy managing directors of SMEs; or people affected by sensitive topics, such as reaching disabled people in accessible design. This makes recruiting participants considerably more difficult.

### Content research

There is also growing demand for content research, as not only how features work but also the clarity of information, the style of communication and the relevance of content are critical for users. Content research helps ensure that products and services are not only intuitive, but also understandable and communicated effectively.

### In-house research platforms

Finally, more and more organisations are recognising the importance of their own research platforms: independent, customisable systems enable faster, more cost-effective and flexible research. They also make operations more scalable and create scope for optimising internal processes.

Together, these trends show that user research is not only broadening but also deepening, gaining ever greater strategic importance in how organisations operate.

blogPosts.title: Daniss-Bodó Eszter: Accessibility is a right, not a good deed
blogPosts.excerpt: I have always looked for work where what I do adds value; I do not stop at making money and producing. I was looking for a worthwhile cause, and for the kind of complexity and balance in which I feel at home.
