After two decades, I finally found all this in UX, while accessibility and inclusive design allow me to draw on both my professional experience and what I have learned from my own life.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Daniss-Bodó Eszter: Az akadálymentesség jog, nem jó cselekedet

content.content:
*In the first instalment of our new article series, Daniss-Bodó Eszter, the newest member of our team, talks about having a sense of purpose, changing careers, the relevance of accessibility and much more. Please join us in welcoming her!*

### I do not stop at making money

I have always looked for work where what I do adds value; I do not stop at making money and producing. After completing my advertising specialisation – and bypassing the obvious agency career path – I worked in other fields. I was looking for a worthwhile cause, and for the kind of complexity and balance in which I feel at home. After two decades, I finally found all this in UX, while accessibility and inclusive design allow me to draw on both my professional experience and what I have learned from my own life.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_akadalymentesseg_jog_nem_jo_cselekedet_1_897166d2e5.jpg
content.caption: Daniss-Bodó Eszter
content.alt: Daniss-Bodó Eszter

content.content:
### With time, I have gained a sense of calm

Until Covid, I worked at a game development studio on a project called Autibarát. Looking back, I was already advocating for accessibility there: as a parent directly affected, I represented the needs of autistic users during the game's development. That was where I first encountered UX and the design thinking method, which completely drew me in. That was when I decided this was what I wanted to do.

After xLabs, I continued learning and began my career in Exalt Interactive's Product Design excellence programme, with support from Klein Péter. It gave me a very useful framework for seeing myself as a junior who also brought more than twenty years of previous work experience. I see age as an advantage: with time and the experience I have gained, I have also found a sense of calm. It gives me a great deal that I have seen many different sectors and systems work – and fail to work – collaborated with many different people, and experienced plenty of setbacks. Having tested myself in numerous roles and environments helps me understand my own limitations and abilities.

### Accessibility should not be just a ‘nice to have’ attribute

I am far more interested in – and concerned about – long-term, higher-level questions and answers. This was one of the topics at a roundtable discussion at this year's Service Design Day, where we explored the designer career path from several perspectives. When we asked the audience, many associated seniority with earnings and status; for me, it is more about the breadth of knowledge and potential that will allow me to guide and move things forward. At one of my former workplaces, the universal saying was: ‘you are a mid-level or senior professional from the moment the client sees you as one’. That is one perspective too.

In the same discussion, we explored what matters most in a designer's career. We concluded that it is *mission.* It is difficult to plan for the long term, persevere, and endure hardship and transitional periods with only short-term goals. My mission is for inclusive design one day – and accessibility until then – to become the default rather than merely a ‘nice to have’ attribute. This requires everyone: from those directly affected, through product development professionals, to decision-makers and the state. I represent two groups here: the designer and the parent directly affected. I have two children, both at different, fluid points on the autism spectrum, and one also has ADHD. I accompany them in their struggles across every area of life, and see the seemingly impossible odds they face in education, employment and even leisure. I refuse to accept that this cannot be improved.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_akadalymentesseg_jog_nem_jo_cselekedet_2_18189064a0.png
content.caption: Career paths in design (left to right): Jaksa Orsolya, Daniss-Bodó Eszter, Klein Péter, Lassú Lilla (Service Design Day, 2024)
content.alt: Karrierút a design szakmában (balról jobbra): Jaksa Orsolya, Daniss-Bodó Eszter, Klein Péter, Lassú Lilla (Service Design Day, 2024)

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_akadalymentesseg_jog_nem_jo_cselekedet_3_6cee6610f6.png
content.caption: Career paths in design (left to right): Jaksa Orsolya, Daniss-Bodó Eszter (Service Design Day, 2024)
content.alt: Karrierút a design szakmában (balról jobbra): Jaksa Orsolya, Daniss-Bodó Eszter (Service Design Day, 2024)

content.content:
### Through one person, you can affect an entire group's quality of life

The quality of life of a child directly affected also shapes that of their family. So when considering what proportion of a country's population is affected by any kind of disability, we should also recognise that, because built, digital and social environments lack flexibility and accessibility, their families and carers are equally affected by the issue, even if not by the diagnosis. Through one person, you can therefore affect an entire group's quality of life, whether that is a family, workplace or other community. This is why we organised the Accessibility Adventure Park at last year's SDD: to connect the design profession with those directly affected, if only for a short time. Under the professional guidance of Klein Péter, Szántai Károly and Nagy Árpád, and with the support of one of the market-leading banks, we created the ‘prototype’ in a very short time. We wanted to provide an opportunity for designers and stakeholders involved in product development to gain first-hand experience of disabilities. It is very difficult to explain in words what it means to imagine that you cannot see or understand something. We created activities across five areas of ability (vision, hearing, mobility, cognitive ability and speech), and invited experiential experts directly affected to help participants in their respective areas by answering their questions. Many people told us afterwards that this kind of approach is needed.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_akadalymentesseg_jog_nem_jo_cselekedet_4_b1e688745a.jpeg
content.caption: Accessibility Adventure Park at Service Design Day (2023)
content.alt: Akadálymentességi Kalandpark a Service Design Dayen (2023)

content.content:
### Disability is a minority group that anyone can join, at any time, involuntarily

At Works., I now focus specifically on accessibility. We acquire some of the knowledge needed for auditing through practice, but there are also online courses on accessibility for different audiences. This is a rich field that affects everyone. It is worth understanding disabilities and conditions of different types and degrees, assistive technology, and the legal and social context – not just the technical requirements.

I am particularly interested in cognitive accessibility, the disability field affecting the broadest range of people. This is why I enrolled in the autism consultant course launched at Pázmány this year. The two-year programme trains professionals who can make environments accessible and educate different stakeholders at large companies employing thousands of people, universities, hospitals, police forces and museums.

The kerb-cut effect applies here too: it can be useful not only for them, but also for people who find communication difficult for other reasons – for example, those recovering from an injury, foreigners, people who struggle with waiting because they are with a small child, older people, or people living with severe anxiety. Disability is a minority group that anyone can join, at any time, involuntarily.

blogPosts.title: “Our colleagues are the stars”
blogPosts.excerpt: On 11 October, Hungary’s service design community came together once again to share their achievements and explore new trends. In connection with the event, we spoke with Maczinkó Ákos and Lichter Tamás, two leaders of the design agency, about the present and future of Works. and the industry.

content.content: /strapi/uploads/sqsp_nalunk_a_munkatarsak_a_sztarok_1_7643e4c21e.jpeg

**On 11 October, Hungary’s service design community came together once again to share their achievements and explore new trends. The Works. team was also represented among the talks on innovation, corporate culture, branding, customer experience, employee experience and service design, with its experts presenting on accessibility and successful telecoms projects this year. In connection with the event, I spoke with Maczinkó Ákos and Lichter Tamás, two leaders of the design agency, about the present and future of Works. and the industry.**

### What was the 7th Service Design Day like, and what would you highlight about the event?

**Ákos:** In my view, it was an exceptionally inspiring, high-quality professional event for everyone involved. Professionals and those interested in the field could choose from a broad range of topics and more than 200 speakers. On a personal note for Works., I would highlight how many familiar faces we were able to catch up with, and how many people came over to speak to us. The event gave me fresh momentum. I felt that, over the past nine years, our team has become an integral part of the Hungarian design community.

**Tamás**: This year’s Service Design Day was both a great networking opportunity and professionally thought-provoking for me. We heard engaging talks and had some good conversations over by the refreshments. We came with three presentations: in two of them, we shared insights from joint projects with our clients. The third focused on a topic that is both timely and evergreen: accessibility, specifically our experience with accessibility audits.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_nalunk_a_munkatarsak_a_sztarok_2_0596026770.jpeg
content.caption: Atmosphere in the CEU atrium — Service Design Day 2024
content.alt: Hangulat a CEU aulájában — Service Design Day 2024

content.content:
### What do you mean when you say accessibility is timely?

**Ákos**: From summer 2025, medium-sized and large companies will be required to make their digital interfaces accessible. We see that the expertise required is not yet available everywhere. The Works. team is professionally prepared for this transition, and four colleagues are already working full-time on accessibility audits. It may sound lofty, but we believe that equal access can make the world a little better. We are also committed to educating the profession, and you will soon be able to find content we have created on our website and social channels.

### How do you see the market? Beyond accessibility, what other changes are you seeing?

**Tamás**: One visible direction is insourcing, especially at large companies. Design departments and customer experience and UX/UI design teams have been established in recent years, bringing some of the work previously done by agencies onto the client side. This is a natural process: as design maturity grows in large organisations, they want to build these capabilities in-house. The challenge can be that these teams need to be nurtured and developed professionally if they are to deliver solutions to a high standard. If a team remains small, training and development are relatively more expensive, and long-term operations become difficult. This is the situation at medium-sized companies, where running design departments may not be financially viable even in the medium term. The teams of up to 20 people that are typical of larger companies are more self-sustaining professionally: knowledge is retained even with lower staff turnover, and businesses of this size have enough projects to support professional development. This trend also means that many people are moving from the consultancy side to the client side, which has a pull effect on talent.

We are seeing other trends too. One is the accessibility already mentioned, while another is a growing demand from clients to shift the focus from consumer audiences to the B2B segment. We, too, are doing more and more B2B research and design work. To mention another conference, FinTechShow took place recently, and its main theme was B2B as a target audience for digitalisation.

I think agencies need to transform and, to some extent, redefine their service portfolios and how they operate. If I look at these challenges positively, I would say they also represent new opportunities, and new types of relationship can emerge with the client side.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_nalunk_a_munkatarsak_a_sztarok_3_2d9ddcd34b.jpeg
content.caption: Anna and Gellért speaking about accessibility at Service Design Day
content.alt: Anna és Gellért az akadálymentességről beszél a Service Design Dayen

content.content:
### Since you mentioned research, what are your further plans in this area?

**Ákos:** Qualitative research related to design is something that is generally not worth bringing in-house; it typically remains on the agency side.

Expectations around research are changing too. There is an increasingly strong demand from clients for companies to recruit respondents for their user experience research from their own customer databases, and to access the learnings gathered from completed research through a company insight database. In response to these expectations, we are preparing to enter the market with software we have developed ourselves. It will be both a major surprise and a challenge for us next year.

### What will this software do, and how will it help?

**Tamás**: We want to create a tool that helps companies manage research they conduct or commission, from the brief through to completion and beyond. More specifically, the tool will make it easy and quick to recruit respondents from an in-house or external database, and to store and retrieve research-related documents in one place in a structured format. Beyond that, our aim is for the software solution to support the ongoing use of insights gathered from research. So we have ambitious goals for the product.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_nalunk_a_munkatarsak_a_sztarok_4_3ba759611a.jpeg
content.caption: Tamás and Ákos in 2017
content.alt: Tamás és Ákos 2017-ben

content.content:
### Turning to the talent side of the design market, what are your experiences of how well prepared design professionals are?

**Ákos**: We see that the client side is already familiar with the fundamentals of design. They increasingly expect more complex knowledge and broader experience from us. So they are more likely to seek mid-level and senior expertise externally. Tamás and I often discuss how, as leaders, we look for adaptability and a generalist mindset in new colleagues, and we train the existing team to develop these qualities too. I think the design profession will change dramatically over the next five years. The winners of this change will naturally be those best able to adapt to evolving market needs.

It has not helped the profession that the continuous stream of design courses is flooding the market with juniors when there is not enough demand for that many professionals. While participants are enthusiastic and committed, in many cases they finish their training only to be left disappointed and without work.

What remains attractive about the consultancy side, however, is the opportunity to gain experience and develop across a wide range of industries and assignments.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_nalunk_a_munkatarsak_a_sztarok_5_5c791b74aa.jpeg
content.caption: Tamás and Ákos in 2024
content.alt: Tamás és Ákos 2024-ben

content.content:
### What is Works.’ strength, and what are you proud of after nine years?

**Ákos**: It is important to us to remain authentic, both internally and externally. We are building a professional studio rather than a “one-man show”. We believe in the team; we do not have stars. We run a self-learning organisation with minimal hierarchy. I think our leadership model is unusual, too. Works. is built around two entirely equal leaders. As neither Tamás nor I have leadership pretensions, we believe more in operating through compromise; the two of us genuinely run the company together.

**Tamás**: Another strength of Works. is that we have several strings to our bow. Rather than specialising in one thing, we offer services that complement and reinforce one another, while also being viable in their own right, such as UX and UI design, qualitative research, accessibility audits and end-user testing. This provides economic stability while offering colleagues excellent opportunities to learn. We have grown alongside the team and the company ourselves, too. We have had some hard knocks, I will not deny it, but they came at the right time and fortunately we learned from them quickly. Quite a few of our partners have remained loyal to us for many years, and that alone is a great recognition for us.

blogPosts.title: Microinteractions — when, how and why?
blogPosts.excerpt: When most people hear the term, they may think of flashy animations, moving loading screens, headers bouncing from side to side, and the list could go on. However, microinteractions are far more than a purely visual element.

content.content:
When most people hear the term, they might think of flashy animations, animated loading screens, headers shifting from side to side, and the list could go on endlessly. However, microinteractions are much more than mere visual elements. They are far more concrete than typical animations, and far more useful than visual movement driven by whim.

Microinteractions help users navigate an interface, making it more intuitive to use and elevating the user experience. They do this through short animations, sound effects or even haptic feedback.

If we were to define them, perhaps the best way to put it would be:

*“A microinteraction is a small response triggered by an action on the interface. In most cases, it is visual, but it can also be sound-based. For it to occur, the user needs to interact with the interface, or the interface needs to prompt interaction.”*
At first, this may sound complicated, but let’s take a closer look:
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_microinteractions_when_how_and_why_1_a021cf05e7.png

**TRIGGER ➡ MICROINTERACTION ➡ FEEDBACK**

These are the three components of a good microinteraction.

In every case, a triggering event is needed to initiate a microinteraction. The microinteraction then takes place and provides relevant feedback to the user.

A trigger can be provided by either the user or the system. However, without a trigger, we cannot speak of a microinteraction. This will become more important later when we discuss what distinguishes a microinteraction from a simple animation.

Let’s look at a practical example:

When a user hovers their mouse over a button, the button’s colour changes. In this case, the triggering event is the mouse hovering over the button. The microinteraction is the change in the button’s colour, suggesting to the user that the button can be interacted with rather than being merely a graphical element. This is the feedback.

Or imagine an email programme. You write your email, click the send button, and the system plays a swooshing sound, confirming that the email has indeed been sent.

**Trigger:** Clicking the send button,

**Microinteraction:** Swooshing sound,

**Feedback:** The email has been sent.

Another familiar example is when a new message arrives in an application and a red circle with a number appears on the application’s icon. In this case, the trigger is the arrival of a new email, the microinteraction is the red circle with the number, and the feedback is that a new email has arrived.

So, we can use them in many different situations, but what exactly are they?

### Feedback on the system’s status:

- Loading screens (the system is loading, not frozen)
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_microinteractions_when_how_and_why_2_e42a99fb72.gif
- Email sent (a swooshing sound or short animation)

- Indication of characters typed (e.g. when entering a password)

### Highlighting changes:

- A checkbox being selected (visually indicating that something has been chosen)
- Toggling a switch (indicating that a different state has been set)
- New message received (a red badge with a number)
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_microinteractions_when_how_and_why_3_cd996e843f.gif

### Prompting action:

- Consent required (a mandatory section is highlighted on the interface, indicating that the user cannot proceed until it has been accepted)
- Guiding users through a process (if the user waits too long during a process, indicate on the interface how they can proceed. For example, the continue button moves or changes colour.)

After all these examples, we may be able to answer the question ourselves:

### What distinguishes a microinteraction from an animation?
“What requires user interaction and helps users understand something more easily is a microinteraction. What serves solely as a visual experience is animation.”

In other words, if we animate an element simply because we think it makes the page look better, it is not a microinteraction.

Many of us surely remember the early 2000s, when enthusiastic web designers filled pages with GIF animations and so much was moving on the interface that it was difficult to make out the actual content among them. Nobody wants that, so let’s use self-indulgent animations with care!

But what about microinteractions? Can we overdo them? The short answer is yes, which is why here are some guidelines to consider when designing microinteractions.

### How to design microinteractions?

- Use microinteractions purposefully; they should support the experience, not overshadow it!
- Nothing should move simply to look "cool". Aimless movement only confuses users.
- Use short, purposeful animations that convey information efficiently.
- A microinteraction is also a design element; it should fit the brand identity and form part of the design system.

And perhaps the most important rule:

"Microinteractions do not replace thoughtful design; a process or interface must be easy to understand, intuitive and easy to use even without microinteractions. Only when the foundation is sound can microinteractions elevate the experience to a higher level."
Happy designing!

blogPosts.title: Issues with parcels
blogPosts.excerpt: A number of issues can arise when shopping online. This article explores the challenges of online shopping, including payment security, delivery concerns and the importance of returns.

content.content:
### Online Shopping & Delivery — Part 5

### Research into the Hungarian market
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_issues_with_packages_1_63ca0242a3.jpg

*In recent years, everyone has experienced how the world of online shopping has changed our lives. The exponential growth of online purchases and the widespread use of online platforms have created new opportunities for businesses, while providing consumers with convenient and fast access to a wide range of products and services.*

*Based on our research into online order delivery, in this series of articles we will present users' expectations and experiences of online order payment, delivery and communication during the process.*

*A non-representative online questionnaire, in-depth interviews and desk research preceded this article. In our questionnaire survey, we interviewed participants between the ages of 16 and 75.*

### Online Shopping & Delivery Series

[#1 — How do we pay online?](https://worksdot.hu/blog/how-do-we-pay-online)

We introduce customers’ preferred payment methods. We explore the criteria they use to make decisions and their attitudes towards increasingly popular virtual card payments.

[#2 — The Economic Effects of COVID-19](https://worksdot.hu/blog/the-economic-effects-of-covid-19)

We discuss the economic impact on online shopping. We look at whether the change in shopping habits during the Covid period has continued, and outline how rising inflation may influence users’ decisions regarding payment and delivery methods.

[#3 — Shipping and receiving](https://worksdot.hu/blog/shipping-and-receiving)

In this article, we look at customer feedback on different delivery methods and preferences. We also discuss how delivery-method choices by product category influence customers, as well as what they think about environmentally friendly delivery methods.

[#4 - Messages during shipping](https://worksdot.hu/blog/messages-during-shipping)

From the moment an order is placed, the status of ordered products and communication related to collection are crucial. In this article, we focus on the messages and notifications customers consider important.

#5 - Package issues and seeking help

In this article, we discuss customers’ perceptions of the safety of online shopping, the items they return, and their concerns and expectations when shopping on international websites.

### Reliability of online shops

A number of issues can arise when shopping online. Beyond the possibility of a faulty or damaged parcel arriving, shoppers also need to consider the reliability of the online shop itself. As the number of online shoppers has increased in recent years, so too has the number of people falling victim to scams. In such cases, shoppers either share their banking details with a third party who then exploits them, or they do not receive the product they paid for.

Our respondents believe that a certain level of digital literacy is needed to recognise phishing emails and SMS messages asking them to share their email address or banking details. This risk is particularly present among older generations, as they spend less time online and have less experience of knowing when, with whom and what data it is safe to share.

Younger generations, who are more active in the digital world and place orders online, tend to be more cautious about the security of a particular online shop. According to our research, people who are sceptical about buying from a certain online shop use digital solutions, such as single-use virtual cards, to avoid payment issues.

A single-use virtual card is a digital card that generates a unique card number after each use, preventing scammers from accessing the full amount.

### General fears about online shopping

Alongside payment security issues, our respondents’ biggest concerns are receiving a faulty or damaged parcel (26%) or not receiving it at all (21%). To address these concerns, online shops should clearly explain how products can be returned.

17% of respondents said they are concerned when they cannot find information on the website about how to return a product. Another common concern is that a product ordered online may not be the same colour or size as it appears online. This was identified as a problem by 16% of our respondents.

On-time delivery is also an important consideration for our respondents. When buying a birthday gift online, timely delivery is the most important factor. 10% of our respondents are concerned that the parcel will not arrive at the promised time.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_issues_with_packages_2_329a52907c.png
content.caption: Chart 1: The biggest fears about ordering a parcel online
content.alt: 1. chart: The biggest fears about ordering a package online

content.content:
### Delivery issues

A common problem is that customers do not see the product until it is delivered. In many cases, they only discover an issue when the ordered product arrives. For example, when buying a fridge, its size and weight mean that the parcel can easily be damaged during delivery, leaving the product dented or scratched.

To avoid these issues, customers like to open the parcel in front of the courier so they can check the product’s condition together and immediately indicate if they do not wish to accept it and want to return it. In the case of a damaged or broken product, our respondents typically expect a replacement or a discount from the seller.

### International parcels

Most respondents have bought products from abroad. They say they are generally more patient with longer international delivery times, but order tracking plays a key role in these cases. They typically have positive experiences with orders within Europe: delivery is considered fast and the parcel usually arrives within the stated timeframe. At the same time, customers consider orders from outside Europe problematic, as delivery takes longer and customs clearance complicates the process. The main inconvenience is that they only receive information about customs clearance once the parcel reaches Hungary, the associated paperwork is complicated to complete, and customs charges can be very expensive.

### Returns

The option to return a product is an essential service for many product types. If returns are not guaranteed, customers can easily stop shopping there and choose another online shop where they are. According to our data, half of respondents have returned a product at least once.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_issues_with_packages_3_fbf1a0f2ef.png
content.caption: Chart 2: Returning products ordered online
content.alt: 2. chart: Returning online ordered product

content.content: Clothing is the product category most often returned by our respondents (35%). This is because shopping in person offers many more sensory cues. In a shop, we can easily decide whether to buy a jumper simply by trying it on, but this is not possible when shopping online. You can feel the material and thickness of a jumper, and see its true colour and shade. Trying it on also reveals how comfortable it is and how it fits. All of this supports the decision-making process. These experiences are limited when shopping online, where decisions must be made based on the images and sizing information available in the online shop.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_issues_with_packages_4_4a193ff328.png
content.caption: Chart 3: Frequently returned product categories
content.alt: 3. chart: Frequently returned product categories

content.content:
Electronic devices were the second most frequently mentioned product category (24%). While the main reason for returning clothing may simply be ‘I don’t like it’, this is not typical for electronics. For these products, returns within the warranty period are the most common. Typical issues with earphones, for example, include not performing as promised, the battery running down quickly, or accessories being easily damaged during everyday use.

The third most commonly returned category among our respondents was sports and leisure equipment (10%). When choosing roller skates, for example, it is important that they are the right size and that the wheels can withstand intensive use on hot summer streets.

Medicines and books were the least frequently returned product categories. These products do not have easily breakable technical parts, and external damage is less significant. Our respondents consider the ability to return goods a fundamental expectation today, so it is essential for any online shop to provide it.

blogPosts.title: Messages during shipping
blogPosts.excerpt: What are the most important notifications and messages when shopping online? From the moment an order is placed, the status of the products ordered and collection-related communication are crucial.

content.content:
### Online Shopping & Delivery — Part 4

### Research into the Hungarian market
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_messages_during_shipping_1_b138fd0f09.jpg

*In recent years, everyone has experienced how the world of online shopping has changed our lives. The exponential growth of online purchases and the widespread use of online platforms have created new opportunities for businesses, while providing consumers with convenient and fast access to a wide range of products and services.*

*Based on our research into online order delivery, in this series of articles we will present users' expectations and experiences of online order payment, delivery and communication during the process.*

*A non-representative online questionnaire, in-depth interviews and desk research preceded this article. In our questionnaire survey, we interviewed participants between the ages of 16 and 75.*

### Online Shopping & Delivery Series

[#1 — How do we pay online?](https://worksdot.hu/blog/how-do-we-pay-online)

We introduce the payment methods customers prefer. We explore the criteria they use to make decisions and their attitudes towards increasingly popular virtual card payments.

[#2 — The Economic Effects of COVID-19](https://worksdot.hu/blog/the-economic-effects-of-covid-19)

We discuss the economic impact on online shopping. We look at whether changes in shopping habits during the Covid period have continued, and outline how rising inflation may influence users' decisions regarding payment and delivery methods.

[#3 — Shipping and receiving](https://worksdot.hu/blog/shipping-and-receiving)

In this article, we look at customer feedback on different delivery methods and preferences. We also discuss how delivery choices across product categories influence customers, as well as what they think about environmentally friendly delivery methods.

#4 - Messages during shipping

From the moment an order is placed, the status of the products ordered and collection-related communication are crucial. In this article, we focus on which messages and notifications customers consider important.

[#5 - Issues with packages](https://worksdot.hu/blog/issues-with-packages)

In this article, we discuss customers' perceptions of the safety of online shopping, the items they return, and their concerns and expectations when shopping on international websites.

### You have one new message

Notifications and emails play a crucial role in online shopping, serving as an important communication channel between businesses and consumers. Timely notifications, such as order confirmations, shipping updates and delivery notifications, keep customers informed about the status of their purchases and enhance the overall shopping experience. Collection-related notifications also play a significant role in the customer experience. The "Successful order" message is the most important for respondents, regardless of the chosen collection method. Customers primarily expect collection-related messages from the delivery company. The least informative messages are those indicating that the parcel is moving between warehouses. Preferences for messages vary depending on the chosen delivery method.

Email is customers’ preferred primary communication channel, especially for home delivery. If delivery takes longer, customers often track their parcels through emails. The "Successful order" message arrives immediately after purchase, but after that, the most important message is the courier’s expected arrival time. They do not appreciate receiving an email notification about the courier’s arrival only on the morning of delivery, as they often cannot prepare adequately. If email communication is sufficiently informative, they do not feel the need for further tracking.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_messages_during_shipping_2_b64a588ba7.png
content.caption: Chart 1: The most important messages about the parcel
content.alt: 1. chart: The most important messages about the package

content.content:
### Messages during food delivery

The digital world has opened up many opportunities in recent years, allowing us not only to buy tech products and clothes online, but also to skip cooking on a lazy day by ordering food to our homes with just a few clicks. Dedicated mobile applications allow users to browse a wide range of restaurants, check prices and promotions, and easily pay online for their chosen meals. However, when it comes to food delivery, expectations vary and customers often prioritise speed. According to feedback from study participants, customers expect their food orders to be delivered within a maximum of one hour of placing the order.

For home delivery, customer preferences regarding messages differ only for food orders. In this case, they primarily expect notifications through the app and do not really follow messages by email. For food orders, the message that the courier has collected the order is considered much more important than in other home-delivery scenarios, as delivery typically takes place shortly afterwards.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_messages_during_shipping_3_fce4d0f53f.png
content.caption: Chart 2: The most important message when ordering food from restaurants
content.alt: 2. chart: The most important message during ordering food from restaurants

content.content:
For collection from parcel points and lockers, the most important information is when the parcel can be collected. Customers find advance notifications or messages about the courier collecting the parcel less informative. Here, too, they primarily expect information by email, but they also find SMS and Viber messages attention-grabbing.

For in-person collection, the message stating "when the product can be collected" is considered the most important after the "Successful order" message.

We were also curious about the channels people currently use to receive order notifications. Of our respondents, 62% believe that, regardless of whether they started their purchase using a mobile application or a browser, they still expect to receive email notifications about every status.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_messages_during_shipping_4_afb48c46fe.png
content.caption: Chart 3: Preferred channels for notifications about incoming parcels
content.alt: 3. chart: The preferred channels for notifications about incoming packages

content.content:
### Where is my parcel?

People track their online orders in various ways, and this has now become an integral part of the modern shopping experience. Consumers appreciate the convenience of monitoring the real-time status and location of their orders, which gives them transparency and peace of mind throughout the delivery process. Whether it is a parcel or grocery delivery, online order tracking increases customer satisfaction by providing visibility and updates on the journey of purchases from the retailer to their doorstep. 
Almost half of respondents focus only on essential statuses, while 33% follow every status notification. Twelve per cent of respondents track their parcel only if it takes a long time to arrive, while 9% pay attention to statuses only for specific product categories.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_messages_during_shipping_5_09d205982a.png
content.caption: Chart 4: The importance of parcel tracking
content.alt: 4. chart: Importance of package tracking

content.content: Age groups also have different attitudes towards parcel tracking. Younger respondents (aged 15–25) tend to follow every status notification because they spend more time online, while those aged 46 and over prefer to follow only the essential statuses.

blogPosts.title: Shipping and receiving
blogPosts.excerpt: The rise of online shopping has fundamentally changed how we live, offering unprecedented convenience and a vast range of products. In our latest article, we explore the complexities of online order delivery, revealing user expectations and experiences through surveys, interviews and research. Join us as we unpack the changing dynamics of sending and receiving in e-commerce.

content.content:
### Online Shopping & Delivery — Part 3

### Research into the Hungarian market
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_shipping_and_receiving_1_e11a2d6d68.jpg

*In recent years, everyone has experienced how online shopping has changed our lives. The exponential growth in online purchases and widespread use of online platforms have created new opportunities for businesses, while giving consumers convenient, fast access to a wide range of products and services.*

*Based on our research into online order delivery, this article series presents users’ expectations and experiences of payment, delivery and communication throughout the online ordering process.*

*This article was preceded by a non-representative online questionnaire, in-depth interviews and desk research. Our questionnaire survey included participants aged between 16 and 75.*

### Online Shopping & Delivery Series

[#1 — How do we pay online?](https://worksdot.hu/blog/how-do-we-pay-online)

We introduce customers’ preferred payment methods. We explore the criteria they use to make decisions and their attitudes towards increasingly popular virtual card payments.

[#2 — The Economic Effects of COVID-19](https://worksdot.hu/blog/the-economic-effects-of-covid-19)

We discuss the economic impact on online shopping. We examine whether changes in shopping habits during the Covid period have continued, and outline how rising inflation may influence users’ decisions about payment and delivery methods.

#3 — Shipping and receiving

In this article, we look at customer feedback on different delivery methods and preferences. We also discuss how product categories influence customers’ choice of delivery method, as well as what they think about environmentally friendly delivery options.

[#4 - Messages during shipping](https://worksdot.hu/blog/messages-during-shipping)

From the moment an order is placed, the status of ordered products and collection-related communication are crucial. In this article, we focus on the messages and notifications customers consider important.

[#5 - Issues with packages](https://worksdot.hu/blog/issues-with-packages)

In this article, we discuss customers’ perceptions of the safety of online shopping, the items they return, and their concerns and expectations when shopping on international websites.

### Online shoppers’ delivery preferences and the factors behind their decisions

Online shopping is an integral part of modern life. Ordering products and services online is convenient, but delivery is essential. The choice of delivery method and provider is therefore crucial to a positive customer experience. Online shoppers have preferences for particular delivery methods and providers, and we examine the criteria consumers use to make their decisions.

### Collection preferences

Our research confirms that home delivery is clearly the most popular delivery method among online shoppers, with most respondents selecting it as their first choice.

Delivery preferences vary significantly by age. Customers aged 15–25 tend to prefer parcel lockers, while older age groups favour home delivery. Younger people are more inclined to receive their orders as quickly as possible, even if it requires more effort. As people get older, convenience becomes a more important factor. In-store collection is the least popular option.

Product categories affect delivery preferences. Prepared meals, household appliances, furniture and groceries are commonly delivered to customers’ homes (e.g. Kifli.hu, Tesco). Parcel lockers are often preferred for books, stationery, beauty products, cosmetics and toys. In-store collection is a popular choice for items such as pharmaceuticals, medical devices, hardware, building materials, and car and motorbike parts. This option allows customers to collect their purchases in person rather than having them delivered.

### Home delivery is the most popular option

Home delivery is often the only option in small towns and villages, where parcel points or parcel lockers are frequently located far from customers’ homes. It is also the easiest way to deliver larger or heavier packages directly to the customer’s door. For example, when purchasing items such as a refrigerator or a treadmill, the back seat or boot of a family car may no longer be enough. Customers have reported that delivery time slots are too broad, which can be frustrating when a courier arrives at an inconvenient time and the customer cannot receive the order. In these situations, customers may ask someone else, such as a family member, colleague or neighbour, to accept the delivery on their behalf.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_shipping_and_receiving_2_b3515d18f8.jpg
content.caption: Chart 1: Product categories most often ordered with home delivery
content.alt: 1. chart: Product categories most often ordered with home delivery

content.content:
### Young people often prefer collecting parcels from parcel lockers

Parcel lockers are popular with urban residents, particularly younger people. Customers pay for the product in advance, so they do not have to deal with payment later.

Respondents prefer using parcel lockers for small, low-value packages. Urban residents appreciate that lockers are easily accessible at any time of day, allowing them to avoid adapting their schedules to the courier's arrival. Parcel lockers are also a good option for customers who prefer discreet delivery, as there is no need to meet anyone when collecting a parcel.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_shipping_and_receiving_3_fc45f027f5.jpg
content.caption: Chart 2: Product categories most frequently ordered to parcel lockers
content.alt: 2. chart: The most frequently ordered product categories in parcel vending machines

content.content:
### Free in-store collection

As mentioned, some product categories are preferred for in-person collection. In these cases, customers expect the product to be prepared and available for free collection in-store. Products often collected in person include fragile items, small but expensive electronics, hardware and medical devices. Customers also consider how urgently they need the product. If the store is easy to reach, they may choose to collect their purchase in-store to get it sooner rather than wait several days for home delivery – especially when buying birthday gifts.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_shipping_and_receiving_4_b3b381c3ec.jpg
content.caption: Chart 3: Product categories most often ordered for in-store collection
content.alt: 3. chart: Product categories most often ordered by personal pickup in store

content.content:
### How do customers choose their collection method?

Respondents considered price, speed and convenience when choosing a collection method. The data shows that the cost of collection is the most important factor across all age groups. However, the second and third most important considerations vary by age.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_shipping_and_receiving_5_656fa398f8.jpg
content.caption: Chart 4: Main considerations when choosing a delivery method
content.alt: 4. chart: Main considerations when choosing a delivery method

content.content:
### Service providers

Our respondents frequently choose home delivery by GLS and MPL, as well as Foxpost parcel lockers. Foxpost parcel lockers are particularly popular among younger age groups, while older groups prefer GLS home delivery. The choice of service provider is typically influenced by the delivery fee. If there is no significant difference in providers' prices, the decision is usually based on convenience. Using the same courier consistently for home deliveries can build a relationship of trust. This may lead customers to automatically choose the same collection option for future purchases.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_shipping_and_receiving_6_54bdb80d64.jpg
content.caption: Chart 5: Most frequently chosen delivery methods and service providers
content.alt: 5. chart: Most frequently chosen delivery methods and service providers

content.content:
### The importance of delivery time in customer satisfaction

Delivery times vary depending on the product or service. Based on customer feedback, prepared meals should be delivered within an hour, while medicines, medical devices and online groceries should arrive on the same day. Clothing and electronic products should be delivered within 2–3 days, and furniture within 1–2 weeks. Customers are dissatisfied when no delivery window is specified or when they are given a full-day window for the courier's arrival. An ideal delivery window is 2–3 hours. For online shopping, a one-hour time slot is the most appealing, but a 2–3-hour window is also acceptable.

Customers expect delivery within the promised timeframe. If there is a delay, they expect to be informed of the additional waiting time. When it comes to food orders, customers are less tolerant and want to know the expected delivery time.

During seasonal shopping periods, such as Christmas, customers may be more patient with delivery delays, but they still expect to be informed in advance. Striking a balance between delivery times and customer expectations is crucial to creating a sustainable and satisfying online shopping experience.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_shipping_and_receiving_7_14b73451c2.jpg
content.caption: Chart 6: Expectations around online shopping before major holidays
content.alt: 6. chart: Expectations related to online shopping before major holidays

content.content:
### Environmental awareness in online shopping

In recent years, sustainability has become increasingly important in both business and society. In response to global environmental challenges and climate change, more and more companies and organisations are recognising the need to manage their operations responsibly. Sustainability has become a key consideration for delivery companies, as their activities contribute to greenhouse gas emissions and other environmental impacts.

Respondents hold differing views on environmental awareness. They primarily expect delivery companies to make changes towards greater sustainability. They believe that optimising delivery routes, consolidating orders and delivering parcels at a later time can reduce carbon emissions.

51% of respondents consider environmental awareness important when receiving online orders, but are unwilling to pay extra for it.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_shipping_and_receiving_8_3b1825935b.jpg
content.caption: Chart 7: The importance of environmental awareness when ordering online
content.alt: 7. chart: The importance of environmental awareness when ordering online

content.content: Companies that use environmentally friendly packaging materials contribute to sustainability. Some businesses already collect shopping bags from previous deliveries, which customers see as a good example. Alternatives to plastic bags, such as biodegradable, recyclable or reusable bags, are already available. Users believe that these small changes can also contribute to sustainability and waste reduction.

blogPosts.title: The Economic Effects of COVID-19
blogPosts.excerpt: We explore the economic impact on online shopping. We look at whether changes in shopping habits during the Covid period have continued, and outline how rising inflation may influence users’ decisions about payment and delivery methods.

content.content:
### Online Shopping & Delivery — Part 2

### Research into the Hungarian market
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_the_economic_effects_of_covid_19_1_355f81ad3e.jpg

*In recent years, everyone has experienced how online shopping has changed our lives. The exponential growth of online purchases and the widespread use of online platforms have created new opportunities for businesses, while giving consumers convenient, fast access to a wide range of products and services.*

*Based on our research into online order delivery, this article series presents users’ expectations and experiences of payment, delivery and communication throughout the online ordering process.*

*A non-representative online questionnaire, in-depth interviews and desk research preceded this article. Our questionnaire survey included participants aged between 16 and 75.*

### Online Shopping & Delivery Series

[#1 — How do we pay online?](https://worksdot.hu/blog/how-do-we-pay-online)

We introduce customers’ preferred payment methods. We explore the criteria they use to make decisions and their attitudes towards increasingly popular virtual card payments.

#2 — The economic effects of COVID-19

We discuss the economic impact on online shopping. We examine whether changes in shopping habits during the Covid period have continued, and outline how rising inflation may influence users’ decisions about payment and delivery methods.

[#3 — Shipping and receiving](https://worksdot.hu/blog/shipping-and-receiving)

In this article, we look at customer feedback on different delivery methods and preferences. We also discuss how delivery method choices vary by product category, as well as what customers think about environmentally friendly delivery methods.

[#4 - Messages during shipping](https://worksdot.hu/blog/messages-during-shipping)

From the moment an order is placed, the status of ordered products and collection-related communication are crucial. In this article, we focus on the messages and notifications customers consider important.

[#5 - Issues with packages](https://worksdot.hu/blog/issues-with-packages)

In this article, we discuss customers’ perceptions of the safety of online shopping, the items they return, and their concerns and expectations when shopping on international websites.

### The pandemic reshaped everyday life

For many consumers, the Covid period brought a shift in shopping habits, with contactless and digital solutions taking the lead. Our research aimed to establish whether the methods users tried during this time have become part of their consumer behaviour, or whether they have returned to their previous habits.

During the pandemic, people had to adapt to restrictions, social distancing and lockdowns, which also changed their shopping habits and preferences.

As a result, shoppers wanted to avoid crowded places and social interaction. This led to a surge in online shopping across all sectors, from food and clothing to electronics. Even for groceries, for instance, more and more people chose to order online to minimise the risk of virus transmission.

Demand for disinfectants, masks and other health products also rose significantly, as people became more conscious of hygiene. Consequently, online shopping and contactless collection proved to be excellent alternatives for those wishing to do everything possible to limit the spread of the virus.

As the virus subsided, shopping habits changed again. While some returned to physical shops and reduced their online orders, a considerable number of customers continued shopping online for its convenience, including for smaller purchases. Buying online also remains popular for products that are difficult to find in physical shops.

### The effects of Covid-19 on online shopping habits
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_the_economic_effects_of_covid_19_2_345a665c78.png
content.caption: Chart 1: Effect of Covid on online shopping habits
content.alt: 1.chart: Effect of Covid on Online Shopping Habits

content.content:
More than half of respondents reported no significant change in their online shopping habits as a result of the Covid pandemic. Fourteen per cent of respondents returned to their previous ordering habits, while a third continue to maintain the online shopping habits they adopted during the Covid period.

### Covid-19 made way for new payment methods
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_the_economic_effects_of_covid_19_3_3beeec88fc.png
content.caption: Chart 2: Effect of Covid on payment method selection
content.alt: 2.chart: Effect of Covid on Payment Method Selection

content.content:
The data shows that, due to Covid, 27% of respondents changed the payment methods they use for online orders in some way and continue to prefer them. Examples include contactless payments, paying when placing an online order, or using payment methods they had not used previously.

We were also interested in whether respondents had adopted new habits as a result of Covid. Our interviews and conversations showed that, since Covid, people shop online and order food more often than they did before the pandemic.

### Effect of Covid on delivery methods
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_the_economic_effects_of_covid_19_4_4555a489da.png
content.caption: Chart 3: Effect of Covid on delivery method preferences
content.alt: 3.chart: Effect of Covid on Delivery Method Preference

content.content:
Delivery methods also changed as a result of the Covid-19 pandemic. Around 45% of our respondents said their delivery habits had changed. Typically, they order online more often and minimise contact with people in crowded places. They also tend to use less cash, arranging tips for delivery drivers online instead. Of this 45% of respondents, 22% have preferred parcel lockers, 18% home delivery, and 5% delivery to collection points since the start of the pandemic.

### Economic impacts

In recent years, shopping habits have been influenced not only by Covid-related restrictions and the consumption patterns associated with them, but also by an uncertain economic climate exacerbated by high inflation.

When we shop in stores or pay our bills, we experience rising prices first-hand. It affects every consumer. While physical retail has typically declined due to steadily rising prices, e-commerce has shifted towards lower-priced products, with no significant decline in the premium market.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_the_economic_effects_of_covid_19_5_8ab7d9f87e.png
content.caption: Chart 4: Effect of inflation on online ordering habits
content.alt: 4.chart: Effect of Inflation on Online Ordering Habits

content.content: Inflation affected the online shopping habits of 43% of respondents. Rising prices also increased awareness and the amount of information sought before making an online purchase.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_the_economic_effects_of_covid_19_6_673a0ccda3.png
content.caption: Figure 5: The impact of economic changes on online ordering habits
content.alt: 5.chart: Effect of Economic Changes on Online Ordering Habits

content.content:
Economic changes have made people more cautious with their spending, resulting in fewer impulse purchases and greater consideration of whether they really need a particular product. When they do need something, they no longer order the first product they find online, but compare prices across several webshops to find the best overall basket value.

Similar shifts in attitude emerged during the interviews. Respondents said they now compare prices more often and pay closer attention to products nearing their expiry date. These products are not only cheaper because they are close to expiry, but can also support more sustainable choices. In addition, respondents said they were open to buying alternative products instead of their preferred brands to save money, for example when buying cosmetics. Minimising costs has also become a priority for online ordering: 15% of respondents look for cheaper, or even free, payment options when making a purchase. Similarly, 15% said they buy less online because of unfavourable economic conditions. A further 10% even postpone certain online purchases.

Recently, consumers have felt the impact of rising delivery costs and are seeking cost-effective delivery options. Many opt for alternatives such as collection points or in-store collection rather than home delivery. If delivery costs are high for a product they have selected online, consumers are willing to collect it in-store to save money.

### Seasonal shopping
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_the_economic_effects_of_covid_19_7_68fde3eaa5.png

End-of-season sales, Black Friday, clearance sales, holiday promotions – the list goes on. Pre-holiday discounts and promotions remain popular with shoppers. 53% of respondents have shopped during these periods, with 26% regularly shopping during discount events. Only 20% said they do not shop before holidays or during sales.

In user interviews, respondents said that they try to shop well in advance of Christmas rather than leaving it to the last minute, as they expect online orders to arrive more slowly at this time of year. Customers are also more accepting of longer delivery times. In these cases, the lack of information is more frustrating than waiting longer for a particular product.

blogPosts.title: How do we pay online?
blogPosts.excerpt: What payment methods do Hungarian customers prefer? We explore the criteria they use to make decisions and their attitudes towards increasingly popular virtual card payments.

content.content:
### Online Shopping & Delivery — Part 1

### Research into the Hungarian market
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_do_we_pay_online_1_5a705e0a99.jpeg

*In recent years, we have all experienced how online shopping has changed our lives. The exponential growth in online purchases and the widespread use of online platforms have created new opportunities for businesses, while giving consumers convenient, fast access to a wide range of products and services.*

*Based on our research into online order delivery, this series of articles presents users’ expectations and experiences of paying for online orders, delivery and communication throughout the process.*

*This article was preceded by a non-representative online questionnaire, in-depth interviews and desk research. Our questionnaire survey included participants aged between 16 and 75.*

### Online Shopping & Delivery Series

#1 — How do we pay online?

We introduce customers’ preferred payment methods. We explore the criteria they use to make decisions and their attitudes towards increasingly popular virtual card payments.

[#2 — The economic effects of COVID-19](https://worksdot.hu/blog/the-economic-effects-of-covid-19)

We discuss the economic impact on online shopping. We look at whether changes in shopping habits during the COVID period have continued, and outline how rising inflation may influence users’ decisions about payment and delivery methods.

[#3 — Shipping and receiving](https://worksdot.hu/blog/shipping-and-receiving)

In this article, we look at customer feedback and preferences regarding different delivery methods. We also discuss how delivery options by product category influence customers, as well as what they think about environmentally friendly delivery methods.

[#4 - Messages during shipping](https://worksdot.hu/blog/messages-during-shipping)

From the moment an order is placed, the status of ordered products and collection-related communication are crucial. In this article, we focus on the messages and notifications customers consider important.

[#5 - Issues with packages](https://worksdot.hu/blog/issues-with-packages)

In this article, we discuss customers’ perceptions of the safety of online shopping, the items they return, and their concerns and expectations when shopping on international websites.

### What payment methods are available to users?

In the early 2010s, cash on delivery and bank transfer were the typical payment methods for online shopping. However, by the end of the decade, the availability of card payments for online orders had increased rapidly with the emergence of online payment providers such as Barion and Simple. This was followed by contactless payment providers such as Apple Pay, Google Pay and PayPal, which allow us to make payments without using cash or a physical bank card. As a result, we can now choose from a variety of payment methods when placing online orders, including cash on delivery, prepayment, online card payments and payment options offered by electronic wallets.

According to the Hungarian National Bank's Payment System Report, the number of internet-based merchants accepting electronic payments increased by 24% last year, giving us access to 42,000 acceptance points for online orders. Electronic wallets also saw significant growth, with the number of cards registered in mobile wallets reaching 1.7 million, representing almost 18% of all bank cards registered in such services. ([source 1](https://www.mnb.hu/letoltes/fizetesi-rendszer-jelentes-20230626-kiemelt.pdf))

### How do people prefer to pay for online purchases?

The payment method chosen for online orders is often determined by individual preferences and age differences. Where customers trust a merchant’s website, online card payment comes out on top. The availability of well-known payment systems on the merchant’s site, such as Barion or Simple Pay, can further increase confidence. This method is quick and convenient, allowing customers to make purchases online easily and securely. Another advantage is that online card payments remove the need to pay on delivery, so anyone can receive the parcel.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_do_we_pay_online_2_8c031fbb46.png
content.caption: Chart 1: Frequency of payment method choices
content.alt: 1. chart: Frequency of Payment Method Choices

content.content: Regardless of age group, most respondents pay for their orders when they place them. While 69% of respondents use a card to pay online, cash on delivery still plays an important role. Bank transfer is the least preferred payment method. This may be because modern payment methods have removed the need for bank transfers, with people choosing easier, faster online card payments over this outdated option. However, preferred payment methods vary across age groups.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_do_we_pay_online_3_b1f979afce.png
content.caption: Chart 2: Distribution of payment methods by age group
content.alt: 2. chart: Distribution of Payment Methods by Age Group

content.content:
Among 15–25-year-olds, contactless payment is more popular than in other age groups, driven by technological advances and the widespread use of smartphones among young people. This generation turns to digital payment solutions primarily for their simplicity, speed and convenience.

Among 26–35-year-olds, online card payments remain dominant, while cash on delivery also plays an important role. The use of electronic wallets is somewhat popular, reflecting this age group’s preference for convenience and positive attitude towards technological developments.

For the 36–45 age group, online card payment remains the most common choice, with cash on delivery also important. The use of electronic wallets is notable, but less prevalent than among younger age groups.

Among those aged 46+, cash on delivery is more popular than in other age groups. For this generation, security and convenience are more important, and they prefer to pay when the product is delivered.

Offering a wide range of payment methods can be a significant cost for online retailers. On the other hand, customers are more likely to choose another merchant if the available payment methods do not meet their preferences. ([source 2](https://www.mnb.hu/letoltes/fizetesi-rendszer-jelentes-20230626-kiemelt.pdf))
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_do_we_pay_online_4_1b27a9541f.png
content.caption: Chart 3: Insufficient payment methods offered by online shops
content.alt: 3. chart : Insufficient Payment Methods Offered by Online Stores

content.content:
71% of respondents have encountered a situation where an online shop did not offer the payment method they were looking for, forcing them to shop elsewhere because their expectations were not met.

This shows that the distribution of payment method preferences can vary across age groups, and businesses should take this into account to meet customers’ needs and support a successful online shopping experience.

### What influences customers’ choice of payment method?
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_do_we_pay_online_5_a66bf8d368.png
content.caption: Chart 4: Factors influencing payment method choices
content.alt: 4. chart: Factors influencing payment method choices

content.content:
Customers’ choice of payment method can depend on several factors. According to the data, the most important factors are the additional costs associated with payment, security and simplicity.

### The cost of using cash

25% of respondents specifically consider the additional costs associated with a payment method. In particular, they look for the cheapest delivery methods and avoid those with higher costs. Where possible, they choose options with no or low delivery and payment fees.

### Security and simplicity

Security is also an important consideration, cited by 21% of respondents. Customers want to use reliable payment methods that protect their personal and financial information.

Simplicity is also important, cited by 16% of respondents. People want to make purchases easily and quickly, so they choose payment methods that are less complicated and easier to use.

The choice of payment method can also be influenced by other factors, such as the delivery method selected or the total order value. Product type may also influence the payment method, although this is less important overall.

### What drives payment choices across age groups?

According to the age group analysis, security is the most important factor for people aged 15–25 and 46+. For these two generations, protecting personal and financial data when shopping online is of paramount importance.

For the 26–35 and 36–45 age groups, the additional costs associated with payment methods play an important role. Customers in these age groups try to minimise these extra costs.

### The world of virtual cards

A virtual card, also known as a web card or internet card, is a digital bank card designed exclusively for online purchases. It cannot be used to withdraw cash or pay at POS terminals. Like a traditional bank card, it is linked to a bank account and contains the essential card details for online purchases, such as the card number, expiry date and CVV2 code.

Many people choose virtual cards because they can load only the amount they need for online purchases, removing the need to provide their primary bank card details on online payment platforms. This minimises the risk of potential fraud or overspending. It is also possible to create disposable or short-lived virtual cards, where the card details expire immediately after payment is made. ([source 3](https://www.erstebank.hu/hu/ebh-nyito/mindennapi-penzugyek/beteti-kartyak/visa-beteti-kartyak/visa-virtualis-bankkartya)) ([source 4](https://www.kh.hu/cikkek/virtualis-bankkartya))

Nowadays, virtual cards are increasingly available from multiple banks, helping to protect people from scams. In Hungary, virtual cards are offered by Gránit Bank, CIB Bank, Erste Bank, OTP Bank, Revolut and Wise. ([source 5](https://tudastar.money.hu/ismerteto/virtualis-bankkartya-igenyles/))
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_do_we_pay_online_6_74eb915952.png
content.caption: Chart 5: Awareness and use of virtual cards
content.alt: 5. chart : Awareness and Usage of Virtual Cards

content.content: According to the data, 37% of respondents have heard of virtual cards, and 39% of them have already used them. On the other hand, 24% of respondents have not yet heard of single-use virtual cards.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_do_we_pay_online_7_dc546b6eaa.png
content.caption: Chart 6: Reasons for using virtual cards
content.alt: 6. chart : Reasons for using virtual cards

content.content:
Among respondents, security was the main reason for using virtual cards. The data shows that 80% of respondents chose this payment method for security reasons. This significant proportion suggests that virtual cards offer customers a higher level of protection, helping to reduce the risk of fraud or phishing.

A smaller proportion of respondents, 12%, said they wanted to try using virtual cards. Simplicity, meanwhile, was the reason only 8% of respondents chose virtual cards.

The data clearly shows that virtual cards are mainly popular for security reasons. This payment method allows customers to protect themselves against potential fraud and shop safely online. As such, disposable virtual cards are an effective and reliable tool for customers making digital transactions.

In the next part of the series, we will discuss the economic impact on online shopping. We will look at whether changes in shopping habits during the COVID period have been sustained, and how rising inflation may affect users’ decisions about payment and delivery methods.

blogPosts.title: Why is lo-fi design important in the design process?
blogPosts.excerpt: How does an apartment floor plan relate to the clay models used in car manufacturing? Both are prototyping methods. We use similar tools when designing digital interfaces, too. Let’s look at which to use and when.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Why lofi design is important in the design process?

content.content:
**What does an apartment floor plan have to do with the clay models used in car manufacturing? Both are methods of prototyping. We use similar tools when designing digital interfaces, too. Let’s look at which one to use, and when.**

The last time we moved house, our family faced the question of where our existing furniture would go in the new place: the bookcase, wardrobe, sofa and piano. We had to work this out well in advance; otherwise, we could not have decided which furniture was missing or what still needed to be bought. Even on moving day, we needed to know where each box was going – otherwise, how could we have directed the friends and family helping us move? So we prepared a floor plan of the new apartment, then cut out cardboard versions of the existing furniture – more precisely, top-down views – to the same scale, and began shifting them around. Everything fell into place – except that we had not considered whether the furniture would fit through the corridor leading to the rooms. But that is another story...
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_why_lofi_design_is_important_in_the_design_process_1_f03e748ad0.jpg
content.caption: Moving furniture is easier on paper
content.alt: It is easier to move furniture on paper

content.content:
Placing scaled furniture on an apartment floor plan is also a form of prototyping – one that saved us time and effort when moving house.

If we had furnished the apartment through trial and error, we would have had to move the piano around quite a lot.

Moving paper cut-outs is significantly faster. The same applies to producing more complex objects: General Motors, for example, has used this method since the 1930s. As a general rule, making a prototype is worthwhile when producing it is significantly cheaper than producing the finished product.

### Prototype types

In our agency work, we often encounter the question of when a prototype is justified in the design process, and at what level of detail. So let us start by clarifying the terms:

### Low-fidelity (lo-fi) prototype

A low-fidelity prototype – or, in industry jargon, a lo-fi prototype or lo-fi wireframe – is a simple greyscale schematic drawing of a website or application that focuses only on the content and structural elements of the layout.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_why_lofi_design_is_important_in_the_design_process_2_47c478c86a.png
content.caption: What a lo-fi prototype looks like
content.alt: This is what a lo-fi prototype looks like

content.content:
*It deliberately contains no colours, icons, logos or other design elements that might distract from the focus on content, navigation and structure.*

Its purpose is to create an early visual understanding of a page or screen, helping the team reach agreement before the creative phase begins.

A lo-fi wireframe is already suitable for illustrating processes and can therefore be shown to management. It can also be used in usability testing with users – although, in this case, feedback relating to the visual appeal of the interface needs to be filtered out.

Experience shows that managers also need to be prepared for the fact that what they see is not the final interface. We have received comments such as, ‘my child could draw better than this’ – which taught us that stakeholders on the client side need to understand what lo-fi delivers and what will come later. The purpose of lo-fi is to model structure and processes; it is as far removed from aesthetics as an apartment floor plan is from the colour of its wallpaper and tiles.

Lo-fi has another clear advantage: it allows development requirements to be estimated with great accuracy.

Of course, changes can still occur at later stages of a project, and the final design may still contain more complex solutions. But these deviations are usually limited compared with the development estimate based on the lo-fi. Having a sound development estimate at this stage is also valuable because it can provide a point at which to stop the project. At first, that may not sound positive in a design company’s blog post, but it is: the investment can be assessed in time to determine whether it is worthwhile. Design costs will also be lower, as there is no need to create a hi-fi prototype if the project can be stopped in time. Completing the lo-fi is a useful decision point. Naturally, it is even better when the project continues, and after the lo-fi stage the team takes a breath before continuing with the hi-fi.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_why_lofi_design_is_important_in_the_design_process_3_f2090caf32.png
content.caption: Full-scale clay car model
content.alt: Life-size car model made of clay

content.content:
**High-fidelity (hi-fi) prototype**

In this case, creating the wireframe requires more effort, as it is a more detailed and complete representation of the final product.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_why_lofi_design_is_important_in_the_design_process_4_a4becf1d24.png
content.caption: What a hi-fi prototype looks like
content.alt: This is what a hi-fi prototype looks like

content.content:
Its purpose is to show how aesthetic features support essential functions.

It is created using clear design elements and, in fact, contains all the elements users will encounter in a ‘live’ environment.

A hi-fi prototype is still ‘just’ a prototype – nothing more and nothing less. In other words, it models the final experience, but it is not yet the final screen design itself, and certainly not a working solution. Usability research based on a hi-fi prototype provides a very close approximation to research carried out on working software. Unlike with lo-fi, the potentially distracting question of aesthetics no longer arises: hi-fi is genuinely very similar to the final screens.

### When we use them

Lo-fi and hi-fi prototypes are tools that can be used in the design process. But it does not always make sense to use both.

Put simply, design tasks can be divided into two cases:

1. A design or redesign affects many areas, and the task is typically of medium or high complexity. It is important to understand early in the project which paths users will take, how individual screens connect, and what information each page should contain. Typical examples include redesigning an entire webshop or designing a mobile application from scratch. In the first case, in our experience, the project typically follows a waterfall model. The team jointly interprets business needs, prepares and validates plans, then arrives at the final designs through several rounds of iteration. The business requirements embodied in the lo-fi and usually documented are then handed over to the development team. This is where the lo-fi wireframe has a genuine place and role in the process.
2. Another typical case is when design takes place within an existing, functioning framework. There is expected to be no need to redesign or significantly transform existing structures; instead, something new is created using existing elements. This might involve, for example, adding a new feature or page type to the existing process or page structure.

More complex tasks can also be handled through agile planning. In our experience, however, creating lo-fi and then hi-fi designs simply does not fit into sprints lasting only a few weeks, so in such cases it is better to forgo lo-fi. An alternative is for the team to plan a separate sprint early in the project to create lo-fi wireframes and think through user journeys.
