In the second case, we rarely encounter demand for lo-fi wireframes. They often simply waste time and add no real value, as the hi-fi wireframe can easily be assembled from existing elements.

### Summary

In summary, lo-fi wireframes are best created when

- new and complex user journeys need to be designed,
- the information hierarchy needs to be clarified,
- it is important to develop a shared understanding within the team or with the project sponsor,
- and the structure needs to be validated before detailed design begins.

There are projects where you can skip lo-fi and start work directly on a hi-fi prototype. But this requires care: it is worth thinking twice about whether lo-fi can really be omitted. Otherwise, you may find yourself in the middle of a furniture-moving project, shifting the piano around the new apartment instead of using scale models cut from paper.

blogPosts.title: How can state diagrams help designers?
blogPosts.excerpt: A state diagram (also known as a state-transition diagram or state model) may sound like an engineering buzzword from the 1980s, but it is a powerful tool that UX/UI designers can use in their projects.
blogPosts.imageAlt: How state diagram can help designers?

content.content:
A state diagram (also known as a state-transition diagram or state model) may sound like an engineering buzzword from the 1980s, but it is a powerful tool that UX/UI designers can use in their projects. In a UX/UI design project, UX focuses on the journey, while UI focuses on states and transitions between them. A state diagram is highly flexible, so you can adapt it to your needs. As a bonus, developers can easily understand it. Let’s look at what it is and how you can use it.

### What is a state diagram?

A state diagram is a visualisation tool “used to describe and analyse the different possible states of an entity within a system” (Business Analyst Body of Knowledge, v3, 2015). An entity can be any object within a system, depending on the system you are designing or analysing. In a design system, the entity is already clearly defined: it is called a component, such as a colour, button, header, table or page.

A state is also a familiar concept in UI design: for example, a button can have a pressed state and a default state. Not all components have different states; a primary colour, for instance, typically has no states, though the components that use it may do. These entities can have states that “do” something either on their own or as the result of a user action. A basket in an online shop can be empty or not empty, a form field can be active or inactive, and so on. More complex components can also have states: a search results list can be empty, and may behave differently in this state from when it contains results.

A component with multiple states may move through them in a predefined sequence, and in most cases the transition from one state to another follows certain rules. For example, in an online shop an empty basket cannot have the “paid” state; it must first contain something. An inactive button cannot be pressed; it must first become active. So when a component has several states, not every transition from one state to another is valid.

In a state diagram, we use boxes to represent states and arrows to represent valid transitions between them. State diagrams are, in a sense, complementary to activity diagrams: in an activity diagram, the boxes represent activities (transitions) and the arrows show states.

Let’s look at an example. We worked on the design for a document management system implementation project for a pharmaceutical company. In this system, a document could have the following states:

- **Edit**: from the moment a user creates the document, they can edit it. Until the document owner sends it for approval, it is considered to be under editing.
- **Waiting for approval**: In this state, the document cannot be edited and is with the managers, who can either approve or reject it. Once approved, it moves to the approved phase. Once rejected, it returns to editing.
- **Approved, waiting for signature**: When all approvers have approved the document, it goes to a further management level for signing. Signatories can still reject it, in which case it returns to editing. Once all signatures have been collected, it moves to the signed state.
- **Signed**: All signatories have signed the document. It can be distributed internally or sent back to the vendor, depending on the nature of the document. It can no longer be edited; it is a “final” version.
- **Invalid**: If a new version of the same document receives all signatures—for example, an internal holiday policy—the previous version becomes invalid.

Let’s see what these steps look like in a state diagram:
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_state_diagram_can_help_designers_1_35afbf25ed.png
content.caption: A state diagram showing an example from a document management system
content.alt: A state diagram showing an example from a document management system

content.content:
### How can we use a state diagram?

All visualisation methods are recommendations rather than rules. We can adapt them to our needs. No teacher is standing behind you to check how precisely you use a state diagram. Business analysts love to standardise their tools, but just because your language has a formal grammar book does not mean you cannot say what you want, in the way you want. Let me show you what I mean.

A state diagram in the format above may seem useful at first, but it is difficult to add other information to it. So first, let’s make it one-dimensional and flatten it. This means placing the states in a single row—it may result in too many arrows around them, but that is the trade-off we make.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_state_diagram_can_help_designers_2_850fb8490c.png
content.caption: A state diagram with the same content as above, but in a “flattened” format
content.alt: State diagram with the same content as above, but this version is “flattened”

content.content:
We can now add another dimension to the diagram, turning it into a matrix. I recommend adding components along the other dimension, so we can show how each component looks in every state. You can simply add a description, or add visual versions to the matrix—it depends on what is easier to understand and create. I recommend including only the components that change according to the states, rather than every component, to avoid making the matrix too large and unusable.

We can also add functionalities along the other dimension and show which user groups have permission to access them in each state.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_how_state_diagram_can_help_designers_3_4076621144.png
content.caption: A state diagram with an additional dimension showing user rights in each state
content.alt: State diagram with an additional dimension showing user rigths in each state

content.content:
This gives us a user rights matrix, and developers will be extremely happy. Another benefit of this user rights versus state matrix is that there are no gaps: since the matrix contains every function and every state, and we have filled in every cell, there can be no special case we have not considered.

The good news is that the two previous matrices can also be combined: states, key components and permissions can all be included in one matrix.

### How do state diagrams help design?

I believe state diagrams are natural tools in the UI design process. In UX, we focus on the customer journey, which is an activity-oriented approach. Once we need to design the final screens, we need to shift to a state-oriented approach: building UI components and defining how each screen should behave. People carry out processes; screens have states. Once we have defined the journeys and screen flows, we need to distil the states of these components. In some cases, these states are straightforward, such as the active and inactive states of a button. For more complex components or processes, however, they are far from straightforward. You therefore need a good tool to collect, describe and visualise these states: the state diagram.

A state diagram is also a quality-control tool: once you have identified all possible states of the main components, you can see whether you have considered every state of the smaller components. Used in this way, a state diagram is a double-checking tool—a framework that needs to be completed.

State diagrams also help when communicating with developers, as they tend to look for gaps in process-oriented designs. Once you have defined every state and every component in each state, there are no gaps—and a happy developer is half the battle.

blogPosts.title: Is the UX designer a dying breed?
blogPosts.excerpt: Do we need more UX professionals with highly specialised UX skills? It is a lively topic of conversation among design professionals. Recent UX trends suggest that the time of resourceful thinkers may have arrived, rather than that of specialised UX practitioners. As a generalist UX designer, I strongly relate to this myself.
blogPosts.imageAlt: Is the UX designer a dying breed?

content.content: Do we need more UX professionals with highly specialised UX skills? It is a lively topic of conversation among design professionals. Recent UX trends suggest that the time of resourceful thinkers may have arrived, rather than that of specialised UX practitioners. As a generalist UX designer, I strongly relate to this myself.
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_is_the_ux_designer_a_dying_breed_mlfg5_1_fa6a8d9f53.jpg

When I decided to become a UX designer, I was overwhelmed by the range of roles out there: UX/UI Designer, Product Designer, UX Researcher, Production Designer. It was clear that I could not land a product design role without experience. But why exactly not?

### I was a skilled consultant and business analyst, working with clients throughout my career on IT and business projects, so problem-solving was practically in my DNA. All the UX courses I took built on this: how to conduct interviews, why to put users first, and how to create prototypes.
**In my current role, I am an experience designer, which is a fine blend of UX researcher, UX designer, service designer, business analyst and project manager.**

I have always explained my role to people unfamiliar with the term UX designer by saying that it is a form of consultancy (as I was a consultant for nearly a decade, this was something my family understood 🙂). Finally, it was a role where I could use all the skills I had learnt as a consultant. I could say I was lucky, but I honestly think that a generalist mindset like mine is what differentiates us from other agencies.

Most of us experience designers at [Works.](https://worksdot.hu/) are generalists. There is a skill set that is essential to this role: being able to talk to clients, conduct user interviews, synthesise problems and come up with possible solutions.
**We help our clients achieve their business goals using UX, business analysis and project management tools and expertise.**
/strapi/uploads/sqsp_is_the_ux_designer_a_dying_breed_mlfg5_2_b1ae069cfb.jpg

1. **UX:** it is essential to be familiar with typical user behaviour, UX principles, design processes, and creating low-fidelity prototypes from simple to more complex. The skills mentioned above are closely linked: UX research and design go hand in hand to create products that users love and use. It is also essential to present these ideas to stakeholders in client workshops, and to articulate our findings and solutions.
2. On the other hand, the role of a business analyst or project manager may seem unusual in an experience designer’s guidebook. **A business analyst ensures that the design meets the client’s expectations** and that the requirements align with the design. We map processes, create [state diagrams](https://medium.com/works/how-state-diagram-can-help-designers-fa13a7f8207f) and produce all the documentation needed to understand the design, so clients can follow it and developers can build the product.
3. **As for project management:** well, this is the thing everyone hates from the bottom of their heart, myself included. For me, project management consists of communication, task management, problem-solving and project documentation, such as meeting minutes and retrospectives. It is hard to imagine working on a design project without these things if you want to deliver it on time.

But this does not mean that we are all equally skilled at writing lengthy business specifications, building prototypes or analysing data from quantitative research. And that is perfectly fine, because we are a team of people with different knowledge and interests.

***Nevertheless, as an agency, we strive to build the core skill set of our junior experience designers from the ground up: research, managing their own time and tasks, and then broadening it further.****Research is the foundation every UX designer can rely on; getting in touch with users and empathising with their needs and problems are key to good UX design.*

The role of the business analyst is often described as a bridge between business and IT. As an experience designer, I believe I bridge the gap between users and clients, while keeping in mind that the design must always be feasible to develop.

**Therefore, the experience designer is more than a business analyst and more than a UX designer combined.** *Of course, this does not mean that a design project is a one-person show, as we all need feedback and opportunities to ideate within the team from time to time.*

Therefore, we ensure that at least two experience designers always work on a project, so they can learn from one another and strengthen each other’s skill sets. One thing is certain: everyone in the design team needs a basic understanding of our users, the business, and design processes and methods, while managing their own projects.

What about UI design? In the agency model, where we work on different client projects in parallel, it is difficult to be both a UX and UI designer at the same time. UI design requires creative work, such as mock-ups and moodboards, as well as the creation of many screens and design systems, while a UX designer needs to focus on the bigger picture: the concept, information architecture, journeys and so on.

**Because of the different approaches involved, rather than the required skill set, it is unfeasible, even impossible, to do UX and UI work at the same time.** *If you are lucky enough to do one after the other, that is fine, but agencies do not typically work that way.*

Someone who only does UX may be a dying breed, as more and more skills are needed to succeed in the field. In the coming years, these roles may disappear altogether as companies begin to realise the benefits of a generalist experience designer. But how can courses and training prepare newcomers for such a challenge? In the next article, we will explore this further.

services.title: UX Research
services.subtitle: EVERY GOOD DECISION STARTS WITH UNDERSTANDING
services.heroDescription: We ground digital decisions in real user insights, so development is based on evidence rather than assumptions.

definitionSection.heading: What is UX research?
definitionSection.description: UX research (user experience research) is a methodology for understanding how users think, feel and behave when using a digital product. Through interviews, testing and data analysis, we gather real evidence so product development decisions are based on facts rather than intuition. The result: less unnecessary development, a better user experience and measurable business outcomes.

intro.heading: What questions can we help you answer?
intro.description: If any of these have come up in your team, research is likely to pay for itself quickly.

cards.title: “We don’t know what to build next.”
cards.description: We help you understand which problems, once solved, create the greatest value for users and the business.

cards.title: “We don’t understand why it isn’t working.”
cards.description: We uncover where users get stuck and what drives their behaviour.

cards.title: “We want to be sure before development begins.”
cards.description: We validate ideas with real users before significant investment in development.

cards.title: “There are more opinions than evidence.”
cards.description: We help you make the best business decisions with objective research findings.

intro.heading: How can we help?
intro.description: We do not offer a list of methods. We tailor the research to the problem at hand.

cards.title: Exploratory research
cards.description: Uncovering user needs, motivations and problems.

cards.title: Concept validation
cards.description: Testing ideas, features and services before development.

cards.title: Improving usability
cards.description: Examining digital interfaces and processes with real users.

cards.title: Understanding customer journeys
cards.description: Analysing the full user journey to identify the most important experience touchpoints.

cards.title: Ongoing research capability
cards.description: Setting up a research system or forming a longer-term research partnership.

intro.heading: How do we work?
intro.description: Five steps that start with a decision and lead back to one. Research with a purpose.

steps.title: We define the brief
steps.description: What decision do you need to make? That guides the research.

steps.title: We select the method
steps.description: An approach suited to the question — no more, no less.

steps.title: We conduct the research
steps.description: Interviews, testing and analysis — conducted systematically.

steps.title: We identify insights
steps.description: We filter actionable patterns from the noise.

steps.title: We support decision-making
steps.description: Prioritised recommendations you can genuinely act on.

intro.heading: What you get from the project
intro.description: At the end of the research, you receive more than just an analysis: you get practical materials that can be used straight away.

smallCards.title: More confident decisions
smallCards.description: Development decisions are based on user feedback, not assumptions.

smallCards.title: Prioritised improvements
smallCards.description: You can clearly see which problems are worth solving first.

smallCards.title: A shared view of users
smallCards.description: A shared understanding of the most important user needs and problems emerges.

smallCards.title: Validated directions
smallCards.description: Concepts and development ideas receive feedback before implementation.

smallCards.title: A better digital experience
smallCards.description: The finished product becomes easier to use, clearer and more effective.

smallCards.title: Research foundations for the future
smallCards.description: Insights and learnings can also be applied to future development.

ctaBanner.heading: Let’s discuss how we can support your project.

projectExamplesIntro.heading: Featured projects
projectExamplesIntro.description: A selection of projects where research delivered tangible business results.

intro.heading: What to clarify before research begins
intro.description: UX research always begins with a specific decision to be made. The project goal, time available and questions to be answered determine which research approach will deliver genuinely useful results. These are the questions that most often arise before we begin working together.

items.question: When is it worth conducting UX research?
items.answer: When a digital decision matters but there is not yet enough evidence to choose the right direction. For example, before launching a new product or feature, ahead of a redesign, when facing conversion issues, or when the team has plenty of opinions but little user feedback. Well-timed research helps you avoid investing time and money in development that is heading in the wrong direction.

items.question: Do you need a finished product or prototype for research?
items.answer: Not necessarily. UX research can be conducted on a finished product, a clickable prototype, an early concept, a service process or even ideas that have not yet entered development. We use a different method when looking for problems in an existing interface than when validating the viability of a new idea.

items.question: How many users do you need?
items.answer: It depends on the research question. In qualitative research, the most important patterns often emerge even from a smaller sample. A larger sample may be needed when examining several target groups, different usage contexts or results that need to be quantified.

items.question: How long does a UX research project take?
items.answer: A focused study can be completed in just a few weeks, while more complex discovery or customer experience research may take longer. The duration is mainly determined by the research objective, the availability of the target group, the methodology and the depth of analysis.

items.question: Can research be conducted online?
items.answer: Yes, online research works particularly well in many research contexts. Interviews, usability tests, concept validation and workshops can all be carried out remotely. In some situations, in-person research provides more value, for example when researching physical environments or in-venue customer experiences.

items.question: How do you choose a research method?
items.answer: We do not start with a method, but with the decision to be made. First, we clarify what needs to be answered: whether we want to uncover new needs, understand an existing problem, validate a concept or identify usability issues. We then select the right research approach.

relatedServicesIntro.heading: Related services
relatedServicesIntro.description: Research is valuable in its own right, but it has the greatest impact alongside our other services.

seo.metaDescription: We uncover real user needs through UX research: interviews, usability testing and surveys. Development is based on evidence, not assumptions.

services.title: UX/UI Design
services.subtitle: Beautiful. Clear. Consistent.
services.heroDescription: We design user interfaces that are intuitive, visually refined and deliver a consistent experience.

definitionSection.heading: What is UX/UI design?
definitionSection.description: UX/UI design is the process of designing how digital products work and look. UX, or user experience, defines how people use the product: the user journey, flows and structure. UI, or user interface, defines how it looks: the visual design, components and details. Together, they ensure that the product is both easy to use and polished, for users and the business alike.

intro.description: If these questions have come up for you too, design is the logical next step.

cards.title: “How can a complex process be made simpler?”
cards.description: We help rethink user journeys so your customers can reach their goals with less uncertainty and in fewer steps.

cards.title: “How can a product evolve without becoming increasingly complex?”
cards.description: We evolve your product so new features do not add complexity, but fit naturally into the existing experience.

cards.title: “How can we design a unified, consistent experience across multiple interfaces?”

intro.heading: What to clarify before we work together
intro.description: No two projects are the same. The business problem, objective and existing operations determine how we work together. These are the most common questions that arise before we begin.

items.question: When should you consider AI-powered digital product development?
items.answer: When you have a specific business problem or idea and are looking for a working digital solution — and want to reach a tangible result quickly. AI is a tool here: it accelerates development and reduces risk, but the focus is always on the problem to be solved.

items.question: Do we need to have a finished specification already?
items.answer: No. It is enough to have a business problem or objective — we will shape the form of the solution together. Often, the first value of a project is clarifying what is actually worth building.

items.question: What digital products do you create?
items.answer: Internal tools, prototypes, automated processes, and data- and customer-experience-driven applications — always tailored to the specific business problem. We do not force a technology onto the problem; we choose the right solution.

items.question: When is AI the right approach, and when is it not?
items.answer: AI is not the best solution for every business problem. We always start by understanding the problem, the process and the business objective — and if AI offers a genuine advantage, we help find the right solution. If a simpler or more conventional digital solution will deliver results faster, that is what we will recommend. As a technology-agnostic partner, we always start with the problem, not the technology.

items.question: Can you work with our existing development team?
items.answer: Yes. In many cases, that is precisely the aim: we accelerate the early, uncertain stage with a validated working version that your own team can develop further and operate. We create the solution in a form that can be handed over.

items.question: What happens once the prototype is complete?
items.answer: We assess the working first version together: what we learned, what worked and where to go next. From there, you can decide whether to develop it further, launch it or hand it over. The prototype is not the end point, but an informed decision point.

intro.heading: What to clarify before an audit
intro.description: No two digital services are alike. The product, your goals and current operations determine how we work together. These are the most common questions that arise before we begin.

items.question: When should we address accessibility?
items.answer: Ideally, from the start of design and development, as this avoids costly redesign later on. But it is not too late for an existing service either: starting with an audit, we can help you achieve accessible, compliant operation through prioritised steps.

items.question: Can we request an audit only?
items.answer: Yes. A WCAG-based audit is valuable in its own right as a starting point: it shows the current state and the most significant barriers. In our approach, however, an audit is not the end point but the first step towards an accessible service — and we can support you with what follows, too.

items.question: Which digital services can you assess?
items.answer: We can assess websites, online shops, customer portals, mobile applications and internal systems. We always tailor the methodology to the product in question and the relevant requirements.

items.question: Can you work with our development team?
items.answer: Yes, and this is often the most effective approach. We work alongside your project team from design and development through to validation, providing specific, actionable guidance — so accessibility becomes part of everyday work rather than a separate task.

items.question: What does the journey towards compliance look like?
items.answer: First, we assess the current state and create a prioritised improvement plan. We then improve the solution together, validate it with real users where needed, and finally help establish sustainable ways of working and internal capability for future development.

items.question: Why is accessibility about more than regulatory compliance?
items.answer: Compliance is the minimum. Accessibility is fundamentally a matter of quality: a well-accessible service is easier for everyone to use, reaches more people and delivers a stronger digital experience. For us, it is not an extra task but an essential characteristic of a high-quality product.

positions.excerpt: Help our clients better understand their users. Through interviews, usability tests and other research methods, you will uncover insights that lead to better digital products and services.

content.content: Works. is one of Hungary’s leading UX/UI design and UX research agencies. We believe that a deep understanding of people is the foundation of good digital products. Drawing on experience from more than 800 research and 200 design projects, we help our clients build on real user needs.

### What will you be working on?
- Planning and conducting qualitative research to support the development of digital products and services
- Using user interviews, survey research and other research methods
- Examining online and offline processes, identifying problems and opportunities for improvement
- Analysing analytics data and user feedback
- Synthesising and presenting research findings
- Developing recommendations based on a user-centred design approach
- Collaborating with designers, developers, product managers and clients

### We’re looking for you if you
- Have at least one year of practical experience using qualitative research methods
- Communicate confidently in Hungarian and English
- Are interested in digital products and services
- Have an analytical mindset and enjoy finding connections
- Think in a structured way and can work independently
- Have strong communication and presentation skills
- Enjoy working both as part of a team and with clients

### It would be an advantage if you have
- Experience in UX Research, Service Design, Business Analysis or Digital Service Management
- A degree in social sciences, economics, design or another relevant field
- Knowledge of usability testing, workshop facilitation or customer journey analysis

### What we offer
- Competitive salary and benefits package
- Additional days off on top of annual leave
- Hybrid working, with at least two days a week in our Budapest office
- Varied projects with leading Hungarian and international companies
- Ongoing professional development opportunities
- An inspiring, supportive professional community
- Laptop, mobile phone and mobile subscription
